article.headline: Kalman Filter Deep Dive — From Theory to OnStep Commands
article.deck: How HYBRID estimates mount drift with a Kalman filter, measures the residual error by plate solving, and converts the result into PulseGuide corrections for OnStep — each step of the cycle and the math behind it.

sidebar.stat_desc: The gain matrix maps 2D measurement errors to 4D state corrections — the dimensional bridge between observation and action.

body.h2_6: 6. A Matrix Dimension Bug and Its Fix
body.p_1: Every telescope mount drifts. No motor is perfectly smooth, no gear is perfectly round, no pier is perfectly vertical. In long exposures this shows up as trailed, elongated stars. The usual remedies are mechanical — better gears, careful polar alignment — combined with autoguiding. HYBRID Telescope Control adds a model-based step: it predicts the drift, measures the residual error, and corrects it while the imaging session runs. The core of this system is the Kalman filter, an estimation algorithm published in 1960 that combines noisy, incomplete measurements into an estimate of where the telescope is pointing — and where it will be pointing five seconds later.
body.p_2: Telescope tracking errors come from everywhere. The worm gear in an equatorial mount introduces periodic error — a sinusoidal wobble that repeats once per worm revolution, typically producing 30 to 120 arcseconds of peak-to-peak deviation. Atmospheric refraction bends starlight, and the amount of bending depends on the star's altitude above the horizon. A star at 30° elevation is refracted 1.7 arcminutes upward; at 10°, the refraction exceeds 5 arcminutes. Temperature changes flex the telescope tube, shifting the focal plane. Wind gusts push the optical tube assembly like a sail. Polar alignment error introduces field rotation that compounds over hours. And the sidereal rate itself — the constant motor speed that tracks the stars — is an open-loop command. It tells the mount where the stars should be, but never checks whether the mount is actually there.
body.p_3: Without feedback, the motor runs, the stars drift, and the only way to check the tracking is to take a picture and look at the stars. HYBRID closes the loop: it plate-solves an image about every five seconds, measures the pointing error, and sends a correction to the mount before the error grows into visible trailing.
body.p_4: The Kalman filter is a recursive estimator. Unlike a batch method that stores all previous measurements and reprocesses them, the Kalman filter keeps only the current state estimate and its uncertainty. Every new measurement updates the estimate, and the old measurements are discarded. As a result, the computational cost per step is constant, regardless of how long the system has been running.
body.p_5: In HYBRID, the state vector has four components:
body.p_6: The position terms capture the current pointing error in arcseconds along the right ascension and declination axes. The velocity terms capture the rate of change — how fast the error is growing or shrinking. Together, these four numbers describe everything the filter needs to know about the current tracking state.
body.p_7: This adaptive weighting is the main difference from a simple proportional controller. A proportional controller always applies the same correction for the same error. The Kalman filter takes into account the history of errors, the expected noise, and the system dynamics, so its corrections include a prediction of the next state rather than only a response to the current error.
body.p_8: Every five seconds, HYBRID runs a fixed sequence of operations. Each step converts the data from one representation to the next, ending with a correction command that the mount can execute.
body.p_9: The plate-solve step is the only point where the real sky enters the system. Everything else is mathematics. The plate solver identifies stars in a short exposure, matches them against a catalog, and reports how far the telescope is from its intended pointing position. This raw pixel error is then converted to arcseconds using the plate scale — the angular size of each pixel, determined by the telescope's focal length and the camera's pixel size.
body.p_10: The filter outputs a four-element state vector in arcseconds. To convert this into a command the mount can execute, HYBRID must translate arcsecond errors into millisecond pulse durations. The ASCOM PulseGuide interface accepts a direction (North, South, East, West) and a duration in milliseconds. The mount firmware interprets these pulses as motor steps at the configured guide rate.
body.p_11: The conversion formula is:
body.p_12: Here, 15.041 arcseconds per second is the sidereal rate — the speed at which the Earth rotates, and therefore the speed at which a perfectly aligned equatorial mount must track to keep a star centered. The division by 3600 converts arcseconds to degrees, and the guide rate factor (typically 0.5× sidereal) determines how fast the correction pulse moves the mount. The result is the number of milliseconds the motor must run at guide speed to close the measured error.
body.p_13: The velocity terms in the state vector add a prediction of future error. If the RA error is currently 2 arcseconds and growing at 0.4 arcseconds per second, the filter expects that by the next plate solve (5 seconds later) the error will be approximately 4 arcseconds. The correction command accounts for this predicted growth and applies a slightly larger pulse than the current error alone would require. This predictive term is the main difference from a basic proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller, which responds to the measured error and therefore tends to lag behind a steadily changing signal.
body.p_14: The standard Kalman filter assumes a linear system — the state evolves according to a linear equation, and the measurement is a linear function of the state. For a well-aligned equatorial mount, this assumption holds reasonably well. The tracking error grows approximately linearly over short intervals, and the plate-solve measurement is a direct linear readout of position.
body.p_15: HYBRID runs both filters simultaneously. The standard Kalman filter handles equatorial mounts, where the linear assumption is adequate. The EKF handles alt-azimuth mounts, where field rotation and refraction create genuine nonlinear dynamics. The fallback to EKF was added after field testing revealed that the standard filter could not converge on alt-az mounts at low elevation angles, where refraction gradients are steepest.
body.p_16: The result was an index overflow: the code attempted to write a two-element result into a four-element array, corrupting memory and producing incorrect state updates. The filter appeared to work when the error was small (because the corruption happened at the end of the array), but diverged when the error was large (because the corrupted values dominated the next prediction step).
body.p_17: Before the Kalman filter, tracking accuracy on the test setups was limited by the mount's mechanical periodic error: typically 5 to 15 arcseconds RMS, depending on gear quality and polar alignment. With the Kalman filter, the measured RMS error was 0.5 to 2 arcseconds — a reduction of roughly five to ten times, which makes longer exposures practical on modest equipment.
body.p_18: The filter adapts during the session. A slow drift or a sustained disturbance is detected within one five-second plate-solve cycle and corrected with a short guide pulse. Disturbances shorter than the cycle, such as a single wind gust during an exposure, are not corrected before they appear in that exposure. Focus shifts caused by temperature are outside the scope of this filter; they are handled by autofocus. The mount does not become mechanically better; its tracking error is measured and corrected continuously.
body.p_19: Each correction cycle has two phases. First, the filter predicts: it uses the velocity terms to extrapolate the state forward in time. If the RA error was growing at 0.3 arcseconds per second during the last cycle, the filter predicts it will be 0.3 arcseconds larger in the next cycle. Second, the filter updates: it takes the plate-solve measurement, compares it to the prediction, and blends them together using the Kalman gain. The gain is a weighting factor that determines how much to trust the prediction versus the measurement. If the measurement is noisy — perhaps because thin clouds scattered the starlight — the gain decreases, and the filter leans more on its prediction. If the prediction is wrong — perhaps because a wind gust suddenly pushed the mount — the gain increases, and the filter trusts the measurement more.
body.p_20: The Kalman predict step uses a simple constant-velocity model. Between plate solves, the filter assumes the error will continue to change at the same rate. The predict step also grows the uncertainty covariance P, reflecting the fact that we become less certain about the state as time passes without a measurement. The update step then shrinks that uncertainty by incorporating the new measurement. The Kalman gain K is computed fresh at each step, adapting to the current noise levels and prediction uncertainty.
body.p_21: Telescope tracking, however, contains nonlinear terms that the standard filter cannot capture. Atmospheric refraction follows a sec(z) law, where z is the zenith angle. The refraction at 80° altitude is not simply twice the refraction at 60° — the relationship is nonlinear. Alt-azimuth mounts introduce field rotation, where the angle between the camera frame and the sky changes continuously as the mount tracks. Mount geometry errors — flexure, orthogonality, tube sag — produce corrections that depend on the current pointing direction in nonlinear ways.
body.p_22: The Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) handles these nonlinearities by linearizing the system equations at each step using a Jacobian matrix. Instead of using a fixed state transition matrix F, the EKF computes F as the partial derivative of the state transition function with respect to the state, evaluated at the current estimate. This produces a locally linear approximation that captures the first-order nonlinear effects.
body.p_23: In an early version of HYBRID's Kalman filter, a single matrix dimension error caused erratic filter behavior. The Kalman gain matrix K has dimensions n × m, where n is the number of states (4) and m is the number of measurements (2: RA and Dec). The transpose of K is therefore m × n, or 2 × 4. When the code multiplied the transposed gain by the two-element innovation vector, the result was a two-element vector. But the state update required a four-element vector — one correction for each state component.
body.p_24: The fix was straightforward once identified: the innovation must be computed as a two-element vector (the difference between the two-element measurement and the two-element predicted measurement), then multiplied by the 4×2 gain matrix to produce a four-element state correction. The dimensions must flow consistently: K (4×2) × innovation (2×1) = correction (4×1). Every matrix operation in the filter was audited for dimension consistency, and a validation layer was added that checks dimensions at runtime in debug builds.
body.p_25: With the machine-learning layer that adjusts the filter's noise parameters, sub-arcsecond tracking was reached in good conditions. The ML model observes the relationship between predicted and measured errors over time and adjusts the process noise covariance Q and measurement noise covariance R to the current atmospheric and mechanical conditions. On a steady night with good seeing, the filter converges to small error bounds. On a turbulent or cloudy night, it relies more on its predictions and applies smaller, more conservative corrections.
body.pull_quote_0: The Kalman filter does not change the mount's mechanics. It estimates the mount's tracking error from measurements and applies corrections for it during the session.

article.headline: The ML + Kalman Hybrid — Predictive Tracking Architecture
article.deck: The Kalman filter corrects measured drift. A machine-learning layer learns how that drift relates to sky position, time and weather, and uses this to tune the filter's noise parameters. This article describes the four-step pipeline, the 24-feature vector, and the safeguards around it.

sidebar.stat_desc: Position, temporal, environmental, and statistical features extracted from each plate-solve cycle feed the prediction model.

body.h2_1: Why ML on Top of Kalman?
body.h2_4: Noise Scaling: How the Filter Adapts
body.h2_6: Results: Before and After Activating the ML Layer
body.p_1: Each mount has its own error characteristics. Some show periodic error that repeats at a fixed period, for example every 480 seconds. Others drift with the wind, or with temperature gradients in the tube that shift the optical axis by fractions of an arcsecond. Autoguiding, the established approach, measures a star's position and corrects the error after it has been observed. HYBRID combines an Extended Kalman Filter with a machine-learning layer that learns how these errors relate to observing conditions and adjusts the filter's internal parameters accordingly.
body.p_2: The Extended Kalman Filter is, at its core, a reactive system. It observes a measurement, compares it to its prediction, computes an innovation, and then adjusts its state estimate based on the ratio of predicted uncertainty to observed uncertainty. This works well for random, uncorrelated noise. But telescope drift is not entirely random. Periodic error is deterministic. Wind gusts arrive in patterns. Temperature follows predictable curves through the night. A filter with a fixed motion model and fixed noise parameters does not use this structure; it responds only to what it has already measured.
body.p_3: A machine-learning model trained on historical tracking data can identify correlations between environmental conditions, mount position, and observed drift. It can learn, for example, that at hour angle +2.5, with humidity at 65% and falling temperature, a particular mount tends to develop a Dec drift of 0.3 arcseconds per minute. The Kalman filter alone would detect this drift only after it had introduced error into the image. The ML layer predicts it in advance and feeds that prediction into the filter's tuning parameters.
body.p_4: The hybrid approach divides the work between the two layers. The Kalman filter handles immediate, high-frequency corrections — the fast loop that keeps stars round during a 120-second exposure. The ML layer runs on a slower cycle, analyzing data accumulated over many plate-solve cycles to tune the Kalman filter's process noise and measurement noise parameters. When the ML model detects that systematic drift is increasing (for example, as a periodic error cycle enters its steepest phase), it raises the process noise scaling, so the filter weights measurements more heavily. When observations become noisy (passing clouds, poor seeing degrading star profiles), it raises the measurement noise scaling, so the filter relies more on its internal prediction model.
body.p_5: The result is a self-tuning filter that adapts to changing conditions during the session. The Kalman filter has no knowledge of the ML layer — it simply receives adjusted noise parameters and responds accordingly. The ML layer never modifies the state estimate directly — it only adjusts the parameters that control how the filter weighs competing information. Because of this separation, the system falls back cleanly: if the ML model's quality drops below the confidence threshold, the filter continues with its baseline parameters, exactly as it would without any ML augmentation.
body.p_6: The hybrid system operates as a continuous four-step pipeline: collect, train, predict, inject. Each step has clear inputs, outputs, and timing constraints.
body.p_7: Every plate-solve cycle — typically every 5 to 30 seconds during imaging — records a feature vector. This is not a snapshot of a single measurement; it is a structured record containing the current RA and Dec errors in arcseconds, the timestamp, the hour angle and altitude of the telescope, the azimuth, and environmental data from the weather station: temperature in degrees Celsius, humidity as a percentage, wind speed in meters per second, and barometric pressure in hectopascals. Alongside these raw values, the system records derived features: the RA and Dec rates of change, the filter's own prediction versus the actual observed error, and statistical aggregates from the last N cycles including error standard deviation, drift trend from a linear regression fit, innovation magnitude, residual norm, and a convergence indicator flag. The session duration and plate solve count complete the vector. In total, this produces 24 features per cycle — a compact description of the telescope's current state.
body.p_8: When the session starts, or when the user triggers a manual retrain, the system feeds accumulated feature vectors into a Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent (SDCA) regression engine. Two separate models are trained: one for RA drift and one for Dec drift. Each model receives the same 24-feature input vector but learns different weight coefficients, because the physical causes of RA and Dec error differ — RA error is driven mainly by periodic error in the worm gear and by atmospheric refraction, while Dec error is driven by polar alignment error, flexure, and wind loading. The training labels are the actual observed drift values from subsequent plate-solve cycles. After fitting, the model reports an R² score — a measure of how much of the variance in the drift data the model explains. An R² of 1.0 means perfect prediction; 0.0 means the model is no better than predicting the mean. The R² score serves as the confidence gate for the entire system.
body.p_9: During imaging, the trained ML model runs on every plate-solve cycle. It receives the current 24-feature vector and outputs the expected RA drift and expected Dec drift for the current conditions. Alongside the drift predictions, it provides the confidence score (the R² value) and the derived noise scale factors: the process noise scale and the measurement noise scale. These scale factors are what the Kalman filter actually uses. The ML model does not inject a correction into the state estimate — it adjusts the filter's tuning parameters, and the filter performs its own optimal estimation with the adjusted weights.
body.p_10: The injection step is where the ML layer connects to the Kalman filter. The system checks the R² confidence score. If R² > 0.5, the model is considered useful and ML tuning is engaged. The process noise covariance matrix is scaled by the ML-derived process noise scale factor, and the measurement noise covariance is scaled by the measurement noise scale factor. If R² < 0.5, the system falls back to the raw Kalman filter with baseline noise parameters — no ML augmentation. This gate prevents a poorly trained model from degrading tracking quality: the model influences the filter only after its R² score exceeds the threshold.
body.p_11: The feature vector is the interface between the data collection pipeline and the ML engine. Each element serves a specific physical or statistical purpose.
body.p_12: The first group captures the telescope's current pointing state and recent error history. RA error and Dec error in arcseconds provide the raw measurement of how far off the current position is from the target. RA rate and Dec rate in arcseconds per second describe how fast the error is changing — a critical input for predicting where the error will be in the next cycle. Hour angle tells the ML model where the target is in the sky relative to the meridian, which directly affects periodic error phase and atmospheric refraction. Altitude and azimuth provide the geometric context for wind loading and gravitational flexure models.
body.p_13: The timestamp in Unix epoch format provides the absolute time reference. UT hour (0 to 24) and LST hour (0 to 24) capture the sidereal time context, which correlates with periodic error phase and the rate at which the mount's gear train rotates. The Julian date fraction provides a continuous time reference independent of calendar boundaries, useful for detecting multi-night trends.
body.p_14: Temperature in degrees Celsius is a major environmental factor: thermal expansion of the mount, tube, and pier all contribute to drift. Humidity affects atmospheric refraction and can indicate approaching weather fronts. Wind speed in meters per second is a main source of high-frequency Dec error, as gusts push the optical tube off target. Barometric pressure in hectopascals completes the atmospheric model, affecting both refraction calculations and the density of the air column above the telescope.
body.p_15: The final group captures the temporal context of the tracking session. Error standard deviation over the last N cycles measures the current noise floor — whether conditions are stable or turbulent. Drift trend, computed as the slope of a linear regression fit to recent errors, captures the direction and rate of systematic drift. Innovation magnitude — the difference between the filter's prediction and the actual measurement — is a direct measure of how well the Kalman filter is performing. Residual norm provides a complementary measure of post-correction fit quality. Convergence indicator is a binary flag showing whether the filter has settled into a stable state. Session duration and plate solve count provide the ML model with context about how much data it has seen. Model age, the time since the last retrain, tells the system whether the model might be stale.
body.p_16: The noise scaling formulas connect the ML layer to the filter. Without them, the ML model would predict drift values that the Kalman filter ignores, because the filter's noise parameters would remain static. The scaling formulas translate ML predictions into filter tuning adjustments.
body.p_17: Process noise scale is computed as: clamp(1 + |drift| / baseline, 0.1, 10.0). When the ML model detects large systematic drift — for example a periodic error peak or a strong wind gust — the absolute drift value exceeds the baseline, and the scale rises above 1.0. This tells the Kalman filter to widen its process noise covariance, so the filter weights measurements more heavily and corrects faster. When drift is small and stable, the scale stays near 1.0, and the filter operates in its normal balanced mode.
body.p_18: Measurement noise scale is computed as: clamp(1 + scatter / baseline, 0.1, 10.0). When observations are noisy — poor seeing, thin clouds, or guide star confusion — the scatter term increases, and the measurement noise scale rises above 1.0. This tells the Kalman filter to widen its measurement noise covariance, which means the filter will trust its internal prediction model more and apply smaller corrections. This prevents the filter from chasing noise, which would introduce more error than it corrects.
body.p_19: Both scales are hard-clamped to the range [0.1, 10.0] to prevent two failure modes. If the scale drops to zero (covariance collapse), the filter ignores all information and the state estimate freezes. If the scale approaches infinity (covariance explosion), the filter trusts everything equally and the state estimate becomes dominated by the most recent noisy measurement. The hard clamp ensures neither extreme can occur, regardless of what the ML model predicts.
body.p_20: The hybrid system must operate safely across multiple threads without corrupting shared state. The WebServer thread calls PredictDriftML on every plate-solve cycle to retrieve the current ML predictions. The UI thread can trigger a manual ForceRetrain at any time. The EKF retraining runs on a background Task to avoid blocking the tracking loop. A modelLock mutex guards the engine swap — the moment a newly trained model replaces the old one, the lock ensures no thread reads a partially-initialized model.
body.p_21: Models persist to disk as zip archives: kalman_ml_model.zip for RA and kalman_ml_model_dec.zip for Dec. The current R² scores are written to metrics.json alongside the model files. When a fresh session starts, the system loads the saved model immediately, giving the filter ML augmentation from the first plate-solve cycle without waiting for a full training pass. The confidence gate ensures this works safely: if the saved model's R² is below 0.5 (perhaps because conditions have changed significantly since the last session), the system simply falls back to the raw Kalman filter until enough new data has accumulated for a fresh training pass.
body.p_22: Before the hybrid architecture was activated, the ML layer existed in the codebase but was effectively inactive. The confidence gate always returned 0.0, the engage condition never triggered, and the filter operated with static noise parameters — no different from a standard Kalman implementation. The table below lists what changed after activation.
body.p_23: With the ML layer active, the test setup reached sub-arcsecond tracking during long exposures in good conditions. The process noise scaling lets the filter respond faster to periodic error peaks while staying conservative during stable periods. The measurement noise scaling keeps the filter from chasing poor-seeing artifacts. Because the model retrains at the start of each session, it adapts to the conditions of that night — temperature profile, wind pattern, atmospheric stability — without manual tuning by the observer.
body.p_24: The architecture is designed to be extended. The 24-feature vector can take inputs from new sensors — a focuser temperature probe, a mount current sensor, a cloud camera — without modifying the ML engine. The SDCA regression can be replaced with another model — a gradient-boosted tree, a small neural network — without changing the four-step pipeline. And the noise scaling formulas can be tuned per mount, per OTA, or per climate, while the overall architecture stays the same. The design keeps a clear separation between what the filter does and how it is tuned, with a learning layer that is retrained as session data accumulates.
body.p_28: R² > 0.5: Model is used only above this score
body.p_29: [0.1, 10.0]: Noise scale hard-clamped to safe range
body.p_32: Background Task: EKF retrains on background thread
body.pull_quote_8: The Kalman filter performs the real-time correction. The ML layer adjusts the filter's noise parameters based on patterns learned from earlier plate-solve cycles.

article.headline: Alt-Az Tracking with an EKF, Compared with PHD2, MountWizzard4 and TPoint
article.deck: PHD2, MountWizzard4, TPoint and HYBRID address different parts of the tracking and pointing problem. This article compares their approaches — feedback guiding, mount model building, pointing analysis and an Extended Kalman filter — with a focus on alt-az mounts.

sidebar.stat_desc: One 4-state model for equatorial mounts, one 6-state model for Alt-Az — each optimized for its coordinate geometry.

body.h2_4: Why HYBRID Uses an EKF for Alt-Az
body.p_1: Elements tracking position, velocity, refraction, and field rotation simultaneously.
body.p_2: Nonlinear atmospheric correction updated every Kalman cycle.
body.p_3: Real-time Jacobian linearization of nonlinear mount geometry.
body.p_4: Machine learning noise tuning activates when model confidence is sufficient.
body.p_5: Alt-azimuth mounts are harder to use for long-exposure astrophotography than equatorial mounts. An equatorial mount aligns one axis with Earth's rotation, which reduces tracking to a single constant speed. On an alt-az mount, both axes move at variable speed, field rotation turns the image across the sensor, and atmospheric refraction bends starlight by an amount that changes with altitude. The common solution is to use an equatorial mount, or an equatorial wedge. HYBRID instead models these nonlinear effects and handles them with an Extended Kalman filter.
body.p_6: Field rotation is the most visible problem. As an alt-az mount tracks a star across the sky, the field of view rotates around the optical axis. Stars do not trace straight lines across the sensor — they trace arcs. After just a few minutes of uncorrected tracking, stars become elongated streaks at the edges of the frame even while remaining sharp at the center. This effect is absent on equatorial mounts where the RA axis is aligned with the celestial pole.
body.p_7: Both axes must move simultaneously at variable speeds. On an equatorial mount, the RA axis spins at the sidereal rate — a constant 15.041 arcseconds per second — and the Dec axis sits still. On an alt-az mount, both altitude and azimuth change continuously, and the rate of change depends on where in the sky you are pointing. Near the zenith, azimuth speed approaches infinity. Near the horizon, atmospheric refraction becomes significant and nonlinear.
body.p_8: Atmospheric refraction compounds the problem. Stars near the horizon appear higher than they actually are, and the correction follows a secant-of-zenith-angle law — not a simple linear offset. The refraction coefficient changes with temperature, pressure, humidity, and wavelength. A static correction table gets you within a few arcseconds, but it cannot track the real-time drift that occurs as conditions shift through an imaging session.
body.p_9: Meridian crossing introduces a change of behavior. At the meridian the altitude axis reaches its maximum and reverses direction, while the azimuth rate peaks — very sharply for targets that pass close to the zenith. For targets crossing the northern meridian, azimuth values also wrap through 0°/360°. Controllers that do not account for these effects can produce tracking spikes or lose the guide star.
body.p_10: A common solution is to use an equatorial mount and avoid these effects. HYBRID's approach is to model the nonlinearities explicitly and let the Extended Kalman filter handle them.
body.p_11: PHD2 is an autoguiding application. Each guide frame, it measures the offset between the guide star and its reference position and sends a correction through one of several selectable guide algorithms — such as hysteresis, resist-switch, low-pass and Predictive PEC. These act much like the proportional, integral and filtering terms of a classic feedback controller, so this article groups them under the PID label. The approach is simple, well understood and widely used.
body.p_12: For equatorial mounts, this works very well. The system is approximately linear: the mount moves at a constant speed on the RA axis, and corrections are small perturbations around that rate. In this regime PHD2 routinely achieves sub-arcsecond guiding.
body.p_13: On alt-az mounts, a guider covers only part of the problem. PHD2 keeps a guide star at its reference position; it does not model field rotation, which on alt-az systems is usually handled by a field derotator or by keeping exposures short. Refraction and geometry effects reach it as part of the measured error rather than as separately modeled terms. Most of its algorithm parameters stay fixed during a session, although the Predictive PEC algorithm learns the periodic component of the error as it runs.
body.p_14: PHD2 is designed for guiding, not for generating the tracking rates themselves. It corrects small errors around the mount's own tracking. On alt-az mounts, those base tracking rates come from the mount controller or another program.
body.p_15: MountWizzard4 is an open-source companion application for 10Micron mounts. It automates building the mount's model: it slews to a series of points across the sky, plate-solves each one, and transfers the results to the mount. The model is then applied by the mount's firmware during pointing and tracking.
body.p_16: For mounts it supports, this is an effective way to reduce systematic errors. A model built from many plate-solved points captures alignment, flexure and other repeatable error terms, and well-modeled mounts can track unguided for long exposures.
body.p_17: The model describes repeatable errors. It is calibrated in a dedicated run and does not re-estimate itself from measurements during the imaging session. MountWizzard4 is also tied to 10Micron hardware, and refraction correction is applied by the mount firmware from temperature and pressure data rather than estimated from the tracking measurements. It is a modeling tool rather than a closed-loop tracking controller.
body.p_18: TPoint fits a polynomial surface to pointing measurements. By collecting dozens or hundreds of calibration points across the sky, TPoint builds a model of the mount's systematic pointing errors, including flexure, gear errors, and alignment offsets.
body.p_19: For pointing accuracy, TPoint is a long-established reference. After a thorough calibration run it can achieve arcsecond-class pointing across the sky, and its models capture spatial patterns that simpler models miss. It is used on amateur and professional telescopes, including alt-az instruments.
body.p_20: A TPoint model is fitted from a calibration run and then applied as a fixed correction; it does not re-estimate itself from measurements during the session. Building it requires many calibration points — typically 30 to 100 — collected over one or more hours. TPoint itself is a pointing-analysis tool; when its model is used by telescope control software, for example by ProTrack in TheSkyX, it also improves tracking, because the tracking rates are derived from the corrected pointing.
body.p_21: HYBRID uses an Extended Kalman filter with a 6-element state vector: RA position, RA velocity, Dec position, Dec velocity, atmospheric refraction coefficient, and field rotation rate. This state captures the essential dynamics of alt-az tracking in a compact, computationally efficient form.
body.p_22: The EKF's Jacobian linearizes the nonlinear mount geometry at each time step. This handles the altitude-dependent azimuth speed, the secant-of-zenith-angle refraction law, and the field rotation geometry without requiring a globally linear model. The linearization is recomputed at every cycle, so it adapts automatically as the target moves across the sky.
body.p_23: The refraction coefficient in the state vector means the filter learns atmospheric conditions from the data itself. No external weather model is needed — the Kalman gain adjusts the refraction estimate based on how well the prediction matches the measurements. The field rotation rate is estimated directly from plate-solve solutions, so no external field rotation model is required.
body.p_24: A machine learning layer tunes the noise covariance matrices (Q and R) based on 24 features including seeing conditions, mount temperature, sky position, and session history. This layer engages when model confidence exceeds an R² threshold of 0.5, allowing the filter to optimize its own noise parameters without manual tuning.
body.p_25: Several properties of the Extended Kalman filter suit alt-az tracking. The Kalman gain balances prediction against measurement: when the model is reliable, the filter weights its prediction more; when measurements are noisy, it relies more on the model. This balance is optimal in the minimum-variance sense when the model and noise assumptions hold. In practice the noise parameters still have to be chosen, which is the role of the ML layer.
body.p_26: The Jacobian linearization handles nonlinear terms at each step without requiring a globally linear model. The secant-of-zenith-angle refraction law, the altitude-dependent azimuth speed, and the field rotation geometry are all nonlinear functions that the Jacobian linearizes locally. This differs from treating the whole system as linear and relying on the errors staying small. The linearization is itself an approximation and becomes less accurate where the geometry changes fastest, such as near the zenith.
body.p_27: The state includes the refraction coefficient directly, so the filter estimates atmospheric refraction from the tracking data. It can therefore run without a weather station, although weather data can still be used by the ML layer. As temperature and pressure change through the night, the refraction estimate follows. The field rotation rate is estimated from plate-solve solutions, so no separate field rotation model is required.
body.p_28: Manual tuning is reduced. The Kalman gain adjusts the filter's behavior to the observed noise, and the ML layer further adjusts the noise covariance matrices based on patterns learned in the current session. The filter starts producing estimates from the first plate solve and refines them as measurements accumulate; it needs several cycles to converge, but no separate calibration session is required.
body.p_29: Each of the other tools is the better choice for some tasks. For equatorial guiding, PHD2 is simpler, well established, and has a large user community and extensive documentation. If you use an equatorial mount and do not need alt-az tracking, PHD2 is the practical choice.
body.p_30: For 10Micron mounts, MountWizzard4 is the specialized tool. It builds and manages the mount's model, which the firmware then applies during pointing and tracking, and it can make unguided imaging practical on those mounts.
body.p_31: For pointing models, TPoint is a long-established reference on amateur and professional telescopes. With dozens of calibration points it reaches a pointing accuracy that a tracking filter is not designed to provide. If your main need is accurate pointing across the sky, TPoint is the right tool.
body.p_32: HYBRID is aimed at alt-az tracking with plate-solve feedback and ML noise tuning. It models refraction and field rotation explicitly and adapts during the session. It is a newer project with a much smaller user base than the other tools, and its published results come from the project's own testing.
body.p_33: The figures below compare reported tracking performance. They describe different quantities and setups, so they are indicative and should not be read as a controlled side-by-side test. On equatorial mounts, HYBRID's Kalman tracking measured 0.5 to 1 arcsecond RMS, compared with typical PHD2 guiding results of 0.3 to 0.8 arcsecond RMS. PHD2 reaches the lower error in this case; the EKF adjusts its weighting automatically, while PHD2's algorithm parameters are set by the user or with its Guiding Assistant.
body.p_34: On alt-az mounts, HYBRID's EKF tracking measured 1 to 2 arcseconds RMS with field rotation correction active. The other tools do not report a directly comparable figure, because they do not target alt-az field rotation in this way and their published numbers measure other things. The ±2 arcseconds shown for MountWizzard4 covers only the modeled error component, and the ±30 arcseconds shown for TPoint is pointing accuracy across the sky, not tracking error.
body.p_35: RMS tracking error with Kalman filter on equatorial mount.
body.p_36: RMS tracking error with field rotation correction active.
body.p_37: RMS tracking error with PID controller on equatorial mount.
body.p_38: Pointing accuracy from polynomial surface model.
body.p_39: On the project's test setups, HYBRID's alt-az EKF tracking came within about a factor of two of equatorial guiding with PHD2, on a mount geometry that is harder to track. Independent comparisons on the same equipment and under the same conditions would be needed to confirm these results.

article.headline: Design Goals and Architecture of a Self-Guiding Observatory
article.deck: How the voice-controlled telescope system and its predictive tracking work: the three tracking layers, the ASCOM and MCP interfaces, the role of voice control, and the current roadmap.

sidebar.stat_desc: Kalman filter for reactive correction, Extended Kalman for nonlinear dynamics, ML layer for predictive adaptation.

body.p_1: Passive sidereal tracking, active Kalman/EKF correction from plate solves, and ML-based tuning of the filter's noise parameters.
body.p_2: Many settings in a telescope control session are changed by hand at the computer: exposure time, target, filter, focus. At low temperatures, with gloves on and dew forming on the optics, each of these changes takes time and interrupts the session, and conditions such as seeing can change in the meantime. Reducing these manual interventions is one of the design goals of HYBRID Telescope Control.
body.p_3: Most telescope control follows a command-and-response model. The user, or a sequence the user has written, tells the mount where to point and the camera when to expose. Drift and focus shifts are detected by measurement — autoguiding, periodic autofocus — and corrected after they occur. Established sequencers automate much of this. For long-exposure astrophotography, where a single exposure can last 10 minutes and a session 8 hours, the approach works, but each correction follows the error it responds to.
body.p_4: Consider tracking accuracy. A telescope mount, even a good equatorial mount, drifts. Periodic error from the worm gear, flexure from temperature changes, atmospheric refraction, wind loading and polar alignment error all contribute to drift that degrades image quality. The standard solution is autoguiding: a second camera watches a guide star and sends correction pulses to the mount. This works well. In its basic form it is reactive — the guide star must drift before a correction is applied — although some guiding algorithms add prediction of periodic error.
body.p_5: Guide star drifts → Camera detects error → Software computes correction → Pulse sent to mount → Mount corrects. Latency: 1-3 seconds. Error accumulates between corrections.
body.p_6: Plate solve measures position → Kalman filter predicts drift → ML layer adapts noise parameters → Correction includes predicted drift → Mount follows the target. Measurement cycle: about 5 seconds. Accuracy depends on how well the model predicts the drift.
body.p_7: The design assumes that no single tracking algorithm covers all conditions. Atmospheric conditions change, mechanical properties shift with temperature, and different mount geometries require different mathematical models. HYBRID therefore uses a three-layer architecture that combines passive, active and predictive tracking:
body.p_8: The architecture was revised during field testing. The Kalman filter's matrix dimensions were corrected, the EKF correction pathway was completed, and the ML training pipeline was extended from single-axis to dual-axis regression. Each change followed a specific failure or limitation found in testing.
body.p_9: HYBRID does not implement its own hardware protocols. It builds on the ASCOM Platform, the widely used standard for amateur telescope control on Windows. ASCOM provides a unified API for mount control, camera operations, focuser positioning, filter wheel selection and observatory automation. HYBRID's ASCOM controller wrapper (1,080 lines of C#) handles GOTO, slew, park, tracking and pulse-guide operations, including error handling and state management.
body.p_10: ASCOM defines how software talks to hardware; it does not define how an AI assistant discovers and calls telescope functions. For that, HYBRID uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It exposes 47 telescope tools through an MCP server, making them available to any MCP-compatible AI assistant. Claude Desktop can discover these tools, read their parameters, and chain them into multi-step sequences. The AI assistant handles the orchestration, and ASCOM handles the hardware.
body.p_11: Voice control is intended to reduce manual interaction during the observing workflow. Typical scenarios:
body.p_12: The Kalman filter predicts mount drift. The ML layer adapts to changing conditions. The scheduler selects targets based on altitude, weather and session history. Decisions within a session are based on the system's own state estimates rather than manual input.
body.p_13: ASCOM commands translate predictions into motion. The mount slews to targets. The camera captures exposures. The focuser maintains focus as the temperature drops. The filter wheel selects the filter for each target. The meridian flip is executed and then verified.
body.p_14: When clouds arrive, the scheduler pauses and waits. When the seeing improves, the ML layer tightens the noise parameters. When a target sets below the horizon limit, the system moves to the next target. When the session ends, the telescope parks and the system shuts down.
body.p_15: Each of these components is implemented in the current version: the Kalman filter, the ML layer, the scheduler, the voice pipeline and the ASCOM interface. The remaining work is integration — making them operate together reliably in real observatory conditions, with falling temperatures, passing clouds, and equipment running unattended through the night.
body.p_16: The development roadmap reflects the progression from voice control to autonomous operation:
body.p_17: HYBRID Telescope Control is MIT-licensed and open to contribution. The source code is available for inspection, modification and redistribution. Open source lets users read the code that makes decisions for unattended equipment, such as a mount running through the night.
body.p_18: The design draws on more than 20 open-source projects: NINA's sequencer architecture, PHD2's guiding algorithms, Stellarium's sky chart rendering, Siril's image stacking, the OnStep community's hardware interface standards, and the MCP ecosystem's tool protocol. HYBRID is released under the MIT license so that its own code is available to others in the same way.
body.p_19: A second goal is to accept complete instructions in natural language. A wake-word assistant can map a phrase such as "go to M31" to a single command. HYBRID is designed to handle a multi-step request such as "slew to M31, plate solve, center it, autofocus, and start imaging for two hours with 180-second exposures": it runs the steps in order, handles errors, and adapts to conditions with limited human intervention.
body.p_20: HYBRID adds predictive tracking. The Kalman filter, a standard estimation method in navigation and control, estimates the mount's drift state from plate-solve measurements and projects it forward in time. Each correction therefore includes the drift expected before the next measurement, not only the error already observed.
body.p_21: Cold-weather operation. At -5°C, removing gloves to operate a laptop is uncomfortable and slows work down. Voice control allows changing targets, adjusting exposures and starting imaging sequences without using the keyboard.
body.p_22: Multi-tasking. While the telescope is imaging one target, you can queue the next target by voice, check the weather forecast, or adjust the scheduler — without interrupting the current imaging session.
body.p_23: Accessibility. Voice input offers an alternative to mouse and keyboard for observers with limited mobility. At public outreach events, it allows telescope control to be demonstrated by speaking.
body.p_24: Multi-step sequences. Commands can be chained. "Slew to M81, plate solve, autofocus, and start imaging for 30 minutes with 180-second exposures" is a single utterance that triggers four MCP tool calls, each dispatched to the ASCOM API. The AI assistant handles the sequence logic; the hardware handles the motion.
body.p_25: The longer-term design goal is autonomous operation: an observatory that carries out the following functions without manual input:
body.pull_quote_3: HYBRID is not intended as a replacement for established applications such as NINA, SGP or APT, which are mature and widely used. Its design goal is a self-guiding observatory: a system that tracks its own state, predicts its tracking errors and corrects them during the session.
body.pull_quote_3_2: Push-to-talk is more reliable than wake-word detection near cooling fans and in wind. A false wake-word trigger could move the mount unexpectedly, so voice input is started by the user rather than always listening.
body.pull_quote_3_3: The codebase comprises more than 200 source files. After the security audit, current work focuses on integration and on the planned roadmap items: multi-star tracking, adaptive process noise, acceleration states, online learning and cross-mount transfer learning.

article.headline: Kalman to OnStep: How a Tracking Correction Reaches the Mount
article.deck: The five-step path from the Kalman state vector to an OnStep rate command, shown with the Python and ASCOM code involved and the timing of each step.

sidebar.stat_desc: Approximate time for one command to travel from Python to OnStep over ASCOM Alpaca. The three requests of a correction cycle take about 150 ms in total; the plate solve (about 2 s) takes most of the cycle time.

body.h2_2: Step 1: Plate Solve — Measuring the Real Error
body.h2_4: Step 3: Python Converts to OnStep Commands
body.h2_5: Step 4: ASCOM Alpaca — The HTTP Bridge
body.h3_5: Method B: Custom Rates — Drift Compensation
body.p_1: Every five to fifteen seconds, the HYBRID Telescope Control system runs the following sequence: a camera captures a star field, a plate solver determines the exact pointing position, a Kalman filter predicts future drift, Python converts those predictions into OnStep commands, ASCOM Alpaca transmits them over HTTP, and the mount firmware adjusts its tracking rate — all before the next image exposure begins. This article traces the complete communication path with the code involved.
body.p_2: The code shows that the Kalman filter never communicates directly with OnStep. It performs pure mathematical computation in Python memory — updating state vectors, predicting future drift, and computing optimal tracking rates. A separate layer of Python code then translates those predictions into two distinct types of commands that are transmitted via ASCOM Alpaca's HTTP REST interface. This separation is the key to understanding how the pipeline is structured and how the measured ±0.5 arcsecond result is obtained.
body.p_3: Every tracking cycle follows the same five-stage pipeline. The stages execute sequentially within a single loop iteration, and the entire sequence repeats every 5 to 15 seconds depending on the exposure time and plate-solve latency. Here is the flow at a glance:
body.p_4: The cycle begins with a camera exposure. The guide camera captures a 1-second image of the star field currently in the telescope's field of view. This image is handed to ASTAP, which performs plate-solving: matching the observed star patterns against its catalog to determine the Right Ascension and Declination the telescope is actually pointing at — the measured position, as opposed to the position the mount reports.
body.p_5: The plate-solve output produces two values: the solved coordinates (actual RA and Dec) and the measured error (the difference between the target position and the actual position, converted to arcseconds). This error is the input to every subsequent step.
body.p_6: At this stage, the system has a measured error in arcseconds. The telescope is off by -0.45 arcsec in Right Ascension and +0.32 arcsec in Declination. These numbers are passed directly to the Kalman filter.
body.p_7: This stage involves no communication at all. The Kalman filter runs entirely in Python memory. It does not open sockets, does not send HTTP requests, does not touch ASCOM. It is a pure mathematical function: given a measurement error and a time delta, update the internal state and compute the optimal tracking rate.
body.p_8: The state vector is four elements: RA position error, RA velocity (drift rate), Dec position error, and Dec velocity. On each cycle, three operations execute in sequence — update, predict, and compute optimal rate.
body.p_9: The update step fuses the new measurement with the filter's prior prediction. The Kalman gain matrix K determines how much weight to give the new measurement versus the existing state estimate. A high-confidence measurement pulls the state toward the observed error; a noisy measurement is trusted less.
body.p_10: The predict step projects the current state forward in time using the velocity estimates. If RA is drifting at -0.09 arcsec/sec, in 5 seconds the error grows to -0.45 + (-0.09 × 5) = -0.9 arcsec. This prediction is the main difference from a simple proportional correction: it estimates where the error is going, not just where it is.
body.p_11: The optimal rate combines three factors: the base sidereal rate, the Kalman-predicted drift compensation, and a proportional correction based on the current error. The correction gain parameter (0.5 = 50%) controls how aggressively the system responds — higher values correct faster but risk oscillation.
body.p_12: Next, the result is translated into commands. The Kalman filter has computed an optimal tracking rate — a single number in arcsec/sec. Python must convert this into two distinct types of commands that OnStep understands. These are not alternatives; both are sent every cycle, in a specific order.
body.p_13: The SYNC command is a standard ASCOM operation. It does not use Kalman predictions at all — it simply tells OnStep the real coordinates. OnStep then recalculates its pointing model, correcting systematic errors like polar alignment drift.
body.p_14: Every command from Python reaches OnStep through ASCOM Alpaca's HTTP REST interface. Python has no serial or USB link to OnStep; it sends standard HTTP PUT requests to a local network endpoint, and the ASCOM server handles the serial connection. As a result, the control software can run on any machine on the network.
body.p_15: The ASCOM Alpaca server runs on the computer connected to OnStep, listening on port 11111. Python sends a PUT request with the command string in the body. ASCOM translates the LX200 protocol command to serial, sends it to OnStep's USB interface, receives the response, and returns it to Python as a JSON object.
body.p_16: The entire HTTP round-trip completes in approximately 50 milliseconds. Two additional PUT requests follow — one for the Dec offset, one for the SYNC coordinates — bringing the total ASCOM communication time to roughly 150 milliseconds for a complete correction cycle.
body.p_17: OnStep maintains these adjusted rates until the next correction arrives. Between plate-solve cycles, the telescope drifts at the corrected rate — which is why the Kalman prediction matters. A simple proportional correction would fix the current error but leave the drift uncompensated. Kalman's prediction of where the error will be in 5 seconds allows OnStep to track at a rate that compensates the predicted drift during the interval between corrections.
body.p_18: The timeline below shows an example tracking cycle, with timestamps for each step:
body.p_19: In this example, the first cycle measured -0.45 arcsec RA error. After 5 seconds with the Kalman corrections applied, the next cycle measured -0.05 arcsec, a reduction of about 90% over one cycle. With SYNC and CUSTOM RATES both active, the steady-state error on the test setup settles at approximately ±0.5 arcseconds.
body.p_20: A common question about this architecture is: why use two methods instead of one? The answer lies in what each method corrects. SYNC fixes the current position. CUSTOM RATES fixes the rate of drift. They solve different problems, and both are needed.
body.p_21: Consider what happens if only SYNC is used, without custom rates. The position is corrected to zero error, but the mount continues tracking at the standard sidereal rate. Over the next 5 seconds, the same systematic drift that caused the original error rebuilds. By the next plate solve, the error has grown back to nearly the same value. SYNC alone only reacts, and has to correct the same error again in every cycle.
body.p_22: Now consider custom rates without SYNC. The Kalman filter predicts drift and adjusts the tracking rate accordingly, but the initial position offset is never corrected. The mount tracks at a slightly different speed, but from the wrong starting point. The error decreases more slowly.
body.p_23: Used together in the correct order — SYNC first to establish the correct position, then CUSTOM RATES to maintain it — the two methods form a closed feedback loop. SYNC resets the error to zero. Custom rates limit how much it grows. On the test setup, the result is a steady-state tracking error of approximately ±0.5 arcseconds, maintained over imaging sessions of several hours.
body.p_24: The system uses a specific set of OnStep LX200 protocol commands, each serving a distinct purpose in the correction pipeline:
body.p_25: When the Kalman filter is not available — for example, during initial startup before enough plate-solve measurements have accumulated, or if the kalman_filter module fails to import — the system falls back to a simpler method. In these cases, a proportional correction replaces Kalman's predictions:
body.p_26: The proportional fallback still sends both SYNC and CUSTOM RATES — the two-method approach is maintained regardless of whether Kalman is active. The difference is that the fallback reacts to the current error only, without predicting future drift. This yields roughly ±2 arcsecond precision compared to Kalman's ±0.5 arcsecond.
body.p_27: The filter is a pure mathematical function. It receives measurements and returns predictions. The translation to hardware commands happens in a separate Python layer.
body.p_28: SYNC corrects position. Custom rates correct drift. Both execute every cycle, always in the same order: SYNC first, then rates. The order matters — rates must be applied to the correct position.
body.p_29: Every command travels as an HTTP PUT request to a local network endpoint. No proprietary protocol is involved, and Python has no direct hardware link. The ASCOM server translates HTTP to serial LX200 protocol for OnStep.
body.p_30: Plate solve: 2 seconds. Kalman computation: 1 millisecond. Three HTTP requests: 150 milliseconds. OnStep application: instantaneous. Total correction time: approximately 2.2 seconds within a 5-second cycle.
body.p_31: If Kalman is unavailable, the system falls back to proportional correction. If ASCOM is unreachable, the tracking loop continues with sidereal-only tracking. In both cases the mount keeps tracking.
body.p_32:
ascom.sync_to_coordinates(ra, dec)

Tells OnStep: "You are at this position NOW." Corrects the position error. Realigns the pointing model. Instantaneous effect — fixes where the telescope thinks it is.
body.p_33:
ascom.command_string(":SXTR,offset#")

Tells OnStep: "Track at THIS speed." Compensates predicted drift. Continuous effect — adjusts how fast the telescope moves between plate solves.
body.p_34: At this point the Kalman predictions become motor commands. The :SXTR and :SXTD commands are OnStep-specific — they set RA and Dec tracking rate offsets relative to sidereal. A +0.068 arcsec/sec offset means OnStep tracks 0.068 arcsec/sec faster than sidereal, compensating the drift that Kalman predicted.
body.p_35: OnStep receives the LX200 protocol commands and applies them immediately to its tracking motor controller. The :SXTR command modifies the RA tracking rate by adding the specified offset to the base sidereal rate. The :SXTD command does the same for Declination.
body.p_36: The recommended commands are :SXTR and :SXTD (offsets) rather than :SX9A/:SX9B (absolute rates). Offset commands are additive — they adjust relative to the current rate — which means OnStep's own sidereal tracking remains active as the baseline. Absolute rate commands would override the sidereal baseline entirely, which can cause issues if the correction is momentarily interrupted.
body.pull_quote_11: Kalman = calculation  |  ASCOM = communication  |  OnStep = execution
body.pull_quote_11_2: The Kalman filter does not communicate with OnStep. It performs pure mathematical computation in Python memory — updating, predicting, and calculating optimal rates.
body.pull_quote_11_3: SYNC says: "Telescope, you are HERE."  Custom Rates say: "Telescope, track at THIS speed." Used together, they reached about ±0.5 arcsecond steady-state error on the test setup.
