sections.tracking_title: 3. Predictive Tracking — Kalman, EKF, and ML

body.h2_4: 3. Predictive Tracking — Kalman, EKF, and ML
body.p_1: NINA (Nighttime Imaging 'N' Astronomy) is a free, open-source application for imaging and sequencing. Sequence Generator Pro (SGP) is a commercial application for automated acquisition. APT (Astro Photography Tool) is a commercial acquisition tool that many beginners start with. All three are mature and actively maintained.
body.p_2: HYBRID Telescope Control is not designed to replace these tools at what they do. Its focus is different: it combines voice control, AI orchestration, predictive tracking, image processing, and remote observatory management in one application, with spoken or typed commands as the primary interaction. The comparison below covers built-in features as understood at the time of writing. NINA in particular extends its functionality through plugins, and the other applications may offer some capabilities through companion software.
body.p_3: Voice control is HYBRID's central feature. A spoken command such as "slew to M31, plate solve, and start imaging for 90 minutes" is translated into the corresponding mount, solver, and camera actions. Three voice backends handle the same commands: Claude Desktop via MCP for cloud AI reasoning, local llama.cpp for fully offline operation, and a built-in Whisper grammar parser as a zero-dependency fallback. The other applications in this comparison do not include a built-in voice interface.
body.p_4: The voice system has its own error handling, spoken feedback, and safety mechanisms rather than only forwarding commands to existing functions. The parser handles 210+ natural language phrase variants across 55 distinct actions. Context-aware stop commands stop tracking, video, slew, or scheduler depending on what is running. Emergency stop is always available.
body.p_5: NINA, SGP, and APT typically delegate guiding to PHD2, which measures guide-star error and sends corrections — a feedback approach. HYBRID adds a 3-layer predictive tracking model: passive sidereal (Layer 1), active Kalman/EKF feedback (Layer 2), and ML-enhanced noise tuning (Layer 3). The Kalman filter estimates the mount's drift and applies corrections based on that estimate, ahead of the next measurement.
body.p_6: Guide star → measure error → send pulse guide correction. Corrects after the error occurs. Latency: 1-3 seconds.
body.p_7: Plate solve → Kalman filter predicts drift → apply correction from the prediction. ML learns periodic error patterns. Corrections do not wait for the next guide frame; their accuracy depends on the quality of the drift model.
body.p_8: NINA focuses on acquisition, PixInsight on post-processing, and PHD2 on guiding. HYBRID covers parts of all three in one application: mount control, camera control, image stacking, calibration, plate solving, scheduling, weather, annotation, and remote web access. The trade-off is depth — NINA's sequencer is more capable and PixInsight's processing more sophisticated. The difference is that in HYBRID these functions share one application and one command interface.
body.p_9: The ngrok-based tunnel with JWT session authentication lets you control the observatory from any device over the internet. No VPN, no port forwarding, no firewall configuration. The 7-tab web dashboard includes live status, image preview with zoom/pan/histogram, remote joystick control, filter wheel and cooler controls, real-time Kalman charts, and a scheduler. PWA support means you can install it on your phone's home screen.
body.p_10: When the WPF UI thread freezes — a rare but possible event during long ASCOM calls or Python subprocess hangs — a background watchdog thread detects the freeze and auto-restarts the application. Session state is recovered from the last 30-second auto-save. The feature is intended for unattended imaging rigs; the other applications in this comparison do not document an equivalent built-in watchdog.
body.p_11: One-click buttons for AI Denoise (a-trous wavelet transforms), Star Removal (morphological opening), and Super-Resolution (bicubic upscale + unsharp mask). When Seti Astro Cosmic Clarity is installed, HYBRID uses its trained PyTorch models. Otherwise, the built-in numpy implementations run on CPU. The acquisition applications in this comparison leave post-processing to separate software.
body.p_12: Nine rejection algorithms for image stacking — from standard sigma-clipping to Linear Fit Clipping and Generalized ESD. GPU-accelerated via ILGPU. SPCC color calibration. Drizzle CFA and mosaic stacking. These are features users typically open Siril or PixInsight for.
body.p_13: NINA's Advanced Sequencer is more powerful and flexible for complex multi-target imaging plans. HYBRID's scheduler is simpler but less configurable.
body.p_14: SGP has years of production use. HYBRID is newer; its code audit found edge cases that more mature software has typically already addressed.
body.p_15: PHD2 is a dedicated guiding application with years of field use across many mounts. HYBRID's built-in tracking is newer and has been tested on a smaller range of equipment.
body.p_16: PixInsight's post-processing is far more extensive. HYBRID's built-in tools are intended for quick previews, not final processing.
body.p_17: The Model Context Protocol gives any MCP-compatible AI assistant access to 47 telescope tools. Claude Desktop can chain tools: "goto M81, plate solve, autofocus, and start imaging for 30 minutes with 180-second exposures" becomes a sequence of goto_target, plate_solve, autofocus, start_imaging calls. At the time of writing, an MCP server is not a built-in feature of the other applications compared here.
body.pull_quote_0: HYBRID accepts 55+ natural-language voice commands and can route them through three interchangeable backends: Claude Desktop via MCP, a local llama.cpp model, or a built-in grammar parser.
body.pull_quote_0_2: HYBRID is not trying to replace NINA or SGP. It is a different interaction model for a different part of the session. Voice control changes how you interact with the scope, not what the scope can do.

article.headline: The Inspiration Map — Where HYBRID's Ideas Came From
article.deck: HYBRID Telescope Control draws on more than 20 existing projects — from NINA's sequencer to Anthropic's Model Context Protocol, from Siril's stacking to Seti Astro's AI post-processing. This map lists what was adopted from each.

sidebar.stat_desc: Telescope control software, AI tools, voice recognition, image processing, and web frameworks that influenced HYBRID's design.

body.p_1: HYBRID builds on work done by other projects. NINA, SGP, and PHD2 had already solved problems that were studied before HYBRID's design was settled. The Model Context Protocol provides the standard that HYBRID's AI-driven telescope control uses. faster-whisper and Silero VAD form the voice recognition stack that the voice pipeline depends on. This article lists where each idea came from, what was adopted, and what was developed specifically for HYBRID.
body.p_2: A free, open-source telescope sequencing application. HYBRID adopted the concept of equipment profiles (save/load telescope+camera+filter configs) and the sequencer's target-based workflow. NINA's plugin architecture showed that a telescope app could be extensible without being monolithic.
body.p_3: A commercial acquisition application known for its session handling. HYBRID's session management (auto-save every 30 seconds, crash recovery) was modeled on SGP's state persistence. SGP's meridian flip logic was studied for the pier-side verification approach.
body.p_4: A widely used dedicated autoguiding application. HYBRID integrates with PHD2 for dither settle and guide-star-lost detection, and also includes its own Kalman-based tracking as an alternative. PHD2's approach to guide star selection and dither patterns influenced HYBRID's tracking design.
body.p_5: HYBRID embeds the Stellarium Web Engine (WASM, BSD 3-Clause) as its in-app sky chart. The real-time sky view, DSS deep-sky overlay, and reticle tracking are all Stellarium technology. The sky chart is HYBRID's most visible borrowed component.
body.p_6: The ASCOM Platform is the standard hardware interface for telescope control on Windows. HYBRID's ASCOMControllerWrapper is an Alpaca HTTP REST client covering mount, camera, focuser, rotator, filter wheel, dome, switch, and safety monitor. Because of ASCOM, HYBRID does not need a custom driver for each mount vendor.
body.p_7: Han Kleijn's ASTAP is HYBRID's primary local plate solver. It runs offline and solves quickly. HYBRID also supports Astrometry.net for cloud solving. ASTAP's hinted-solve mode (using the mount's approximate position) was adopted for speed.
body.p_8: The Model Context Protocol is Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI assistants to external tools. HYBRID's 47 MCP tools follow this standard. Claude Desktop is the primary voice backend — it interprets telescope commands and chains MCP tool calls.
body.p_9: The CTranslate2 port of OpenAI's Whisper model. HYBRID uses the small.en variant for near-real-time transcription. Silero VAD (from the same ecosystem) handles voice activity detection. Together they form the core of HYBRID's voice input pipeline.
body.p_10: The local LLM backends that make fully offline voice control possible. HYBRID's llama.cpp bridge connects to a local Qwen3 model for remote observatories without internet. Ollama provides a simpler alternative for users who prefer its model management.
body.p_11: HYBRID includes a voice bridge for VS Code Copilot Chat, allowing developers to control the telescope from their editor. The bridge was modeled after Claude Desktop's MCP integration but adapted for Copilot's different protocol.
body.p_12: The free, open-source astro image processor. HYBRID's stacking algorithms (sigma-clipping, Winsorized, median) were validated against Siril's output. Siril's background extraction (RBF thin-plate spline + polynomial) was studied for HYBRID's BackgroundExtractionEngine. Siril 1.4.2 source was included in build staging for reference.
body.p_13: The professional standard for astro image processing. HYBRID's SPCC color calibration and drizzle algorithms reference PixInsight's approach. HYBRID's post-processing is positioned as a preview tool — users are expected to take HYBRID's linear masters into PixInsight for final production.
body.p_14: The original source of the AI Denoise, Star Removal, and Super-Resolution algorithms. HYBRID's numpy implementations were reimplemented from scratch based on SASpro's reference scripts. When Seti Astro Cosmic Clarity (trained PyTorch models) is installed, HYBRID uses those instead.
body.p_15: SharpCap's live-stacking behavior (Winsorized rejection, automatic background neutralization) was used as a reference for HYBRID's stacking engine. The dev log explicitly notes that HYBRID's winsorize behavior "matches SharpCap."
body.p_16: Three features have no direct counterpart in the telescope software reviewed for this project. First, conversational voice control with AI orchestration. The voice pipeline (microphone → VAD → STT → parser → MCP dispatch → ASCOM command) was designed specifically for HYBRID, because the existing voice integrations for hardware control that were reviewed did not handle astronomical commands.
body.p_17: Second, the 3-layer predictive tracking model (sidereal + Kalman/EKF + ML). PHD2's guiding works by feedback: it measures the error, then corrects it. HYBRID's tracking is predictive — it uses a Kalman filter to estimate the mount's drift state and applies corrections based on that estimate. The ML layer learns periodic error patterns over time. The approach is common in aerospace and robotics and less common in amateur astronomy software.
body.p_18: Third, the UI-freeze watchdog with auto-restart and session recovery is a reliability feature borrowed from industrial control systems rather than telescope software. A background thread monitors the UI thread's responsiveness; if it freezes beyond a configurable threshold (default 45 seconds), the watchdog kills and restarts the application, recovering state from the last auto-save. It is intended for unattended imaging rigs running for 6+ hours.
body.p_19: Primary IDE. MSBuild Release|x64 via BUILD.bat. SDK-style .csproj with auto-include. C# 7.3 language version.
body.p_20: Installer pipeline: NSIS compile → stage ~4.9 GB → 7z LZMA2 → SFX. Output: single ~2.64 GB EXE.
body.p_21: 347+ unit tests across GUI (161), ImageProcessing (357), Camera (34), and WebUI (25 Playwright). Hardware-independent regression tests.
body.p_22: Website build (Vite + TypeScript). Server-side analytics (server_with_analytics.cjs). Deployed via SCP/SSH.
body.pull_quote_0: HYBRID's voice pipeline was designed for this project rather than adapted from an existing telescope tool. The nearest comparison is voice-controlled home automation, but moving a telescope has stricter safety requirements than switching on a light, which is why the pipeline includes context-aware stop commands and an always-available emergency stop.

article.headline: The 48 Features — A Complete Catalog of Every Capability
article.deck: From plate solving to dome automation, from voice control to PEC analysis — every capability of the voice-controlled observatory, cataloged and explained.

sidebar.stat_desc: Organized across 8 categories: Tracking, Voice, Imaging, Session, System, Processing, Remote, and Integration.

body.p_1: HYBRID Telescope Control combines mount tracking with voice input, plate solving, automatic error correction, and control of the other observatory subsystems from a single laptop. This catalog documents its forty-eight discrete features, from Kalman-filter predictive tracking to voice commands in two languages.
body.p_2: The standard HYBRID package ships with 41 features covering tracking, imaging, automation, and system management. The Pro tier adds seven capabilities that extend HYBRID from telescope control to observatory equipment such as domes, power switches, and flat panels. Each one interfaces with an external hardware protocol and has its own state management.
body.p_3: INDI and Alpaca dome protocol support. The dome shutter, rotation, and home index are tracked in real time. Park, track, and wire modes allow the dome to follow the mount through meridian flips and target switches without manual intervention. Auto sync keeps the dome slit aligned with the telescope's optical axis during the session.
body.p_4: Four-channel relay management with per-switch naming, auto-off timers, and a live power budget display. Each switch can be assigned to a subsystem — mount, camera, dew heater, focuser — and configured with independent on/off schedules. The power budget tracker prevents overloads by monitoring total draw against supply capacity.
body.p_5: Absolute positioning with backlash compensation in both directions. Auto focus routines use HFR (half-flux radius) measurement to find the critical focus zone. Filter offsets allow refocusing when switching between narrowband and broadband filters without repeating the full autofocus cycle.
body.p_6: Angle synchronization keeps the camera oriented correctly relative to the target throughout long exposures. Meridian flip rotation compensates for the 180-degree image rotation that occurs during pier-side transitions. Framing presets store preferred position angles for common targets.
body.p_7: Flat panel control for calibration frames. The system manages panel brightness, exposure duration, and session planning for dusk/dawn flats. Integration with the sequence engine allows automated flat frames at session start or end.
body.p_8: A plate-solve-based routine modeled on the TVC (Takahashi Variation Correction) method. It targets a polar alignment accuracy of plus or minus 5 arcseconds through iterative star measurements and mount offset calculations. No additional hardware is required beyond the main imaging camera.
body.p_9: A single command that frames a target by centering it in the field and rotating the camera to the desired position angle. The system plate-solves, calculates the offset, slews the mount, and rotates the camera in sequence — all without user intervention.
body.p_10: The tracking stack underpins the other features: image quality and automation both depend on accurate tracking. HYBRID implements twelve distinct tracking subsystems that work together.
body.p_11: A 4×4 state-space model tracking RA position, RA velocity, Dec position, and Dec velocity. The filter fuses mount encoder readings with plate-solve corrections to produce a predicted state that smooths out periodic error, backlash, and atmospheric refraction artifacts. An extended Kalman filter variant handles nonlinear Jacobian matrices when tracking rates deviate significantly from sidereal.
body.p_12: Direct integration with OnStepX via serial and network connections. INDI drivers provide an abstraction layer for mounts, cameras, and accessories. Both paths are supported simultaneously — a user can run OnStepX on a Raspberry Pi while the Windows laptop handles image processing and scheduling.
body.p_13: Standard ASCOM PulseGuide interface with 100-millisecond pulse resolution on both RA and Dec axes. Compatible with PHD2, MetaGuide, and any other guiding application that speaks ASCOM.
body.p_14: Over 3,000 objects with magnitude, seasonal visibility, and current altitude data. The catalog is queried in real time to suggest targets based on observability windows, moon illumination, and user preferences.
body.p_15: Powered by astrometry.net, the plate solver can recover pointing without a position hint, including when the mount's position is unknown. Solve times range from 2 seconds for well-exposed star fields to 30 seconds for faint-field solutions.
body.p_16: A 5-second cadence plate-solve loop that continuously syncs the mount's reported position with the actual sky coordinates. The feedback is fed back into the Kalman filter, creating a closed-loop tracking system that corrects drift in real time.
body.p_17: FFT analysis of tracking errors reveals the worm gear's periodic signature. HYBRID captures the error waveform, fits a correction curve, and exports it directly to OnStepX for hardware-level PEC playback. The aim is sub-arcsecond tracking without autoguiding; the achieved result depends on the mount and the seeing.
body.p_18: HYBRID ships voice control as a working production feature rather than a demo. It handles 210+ phrase variants across 55+ actions in French and English, with support for ten or more dialects.
body.p_19: OpenAI Whisper large-v3 runs locally on the GPU for sub-second transcription. A Silero VAD (voice activity detection) combined with an energy gate provides dual-layer noise filtering that rejects wind, traffic, and dew heater hum without clipping speech.
body.p_20: Every major subsystem is voice-controllable: slew to target, start imaging, run autofocus, check weather, park the mount, open the dome. Commands are parsed with fuzzy matching — "point at Andromeda" and "slew to M31" both resolve to the same target.
body.p_21: Local processing for low-latency control. Gemini CLI for conversational target selection and session planning. Claude CLI for complex multi-step commands and natural language scripting. Users can switch backends mid-session based on connectivity and complexity.
body.p_22: 47 tools exposed via Model Context Protocol with OpenAI function calling format. Any LLM that supports function calling can control the telescope — not just the built-in backends.
body.p_23: FITS image processing is a core part of HYBRID. Fifteen distinct analysis methods cover everything from basic statistics to star shape characterization.
body.p_24: HFR-based filtering with quality grades A through D. Frames exceeding the user-defined FWHM or eccentricity thresholds are automatically rejected before stacking. This removes frames with trailing, bloated stars, or clouds without manual inspection.
body.p_25: Automatic background modeling using mesh interpolation. The extracted background is subtracted from each frame, removing gradient artifacts from light pollution, moon glow, and vignetting.
body.p_26: Three stacking algorithms: median for maximum outlier rejection, mean for best signal-to-noise, and sigma-clipped mean for a balance of both. Stacks update in real time as new frames arrive, producing a progressively deeper image throughout the session.
body.p_27: 8-bit preview images exported as PNG, JPEG, or TIFF for quick sharing. The full 16-bit or 32-bit FITS data is preserved separately for scientific processing.
body.p_28: An observatory session is a sequence of decisions, adjustments, and contingencies that unfold over hours. HYBRID automates the main steps of that workflow.
body.p_29: Targets are queued with altitude constraints, moon avoidance windows, and priority scores. The scheduler reorders the queue in real time as conditions change — a target rising above the horizon takes precedence over one sinking behind trees.
body.p_30: When the mount approaches the meridian, HYBRID pauses imaging, verifies pier side, flips the mount, re-centers the target, and resumes — without user intervention. The plate-solve feedback loop is designed to re-acquire the target within 2 arcseconds of its pre-flip position.
body.p_31: PHD2 integration via ASCOM. Dithering between frames reduces walking noise patterns. Guiding calibration is automated at session start, and guide star selection uses the same HFR metrics as the main imaging pipeline.
body.p_32: N-step sequences with loops, conditional logic, and sub-frame selection. A typical sequence might be: 20×300s L, 15×300s R, 15×300s G, 15×300s B, each with autofocus triggers every 10 frames and flat calibration between filter changes.
body.p_33: Weather data from OpenWeatherMap and Meteoblue is polled continuously. Wind speed, cloud cover, and humidity thresholds trigger automatic session abort. The safety monitor is independent of the main control loop — it cannot be overridden by voice commands or automation scripts.
body.p_34: The remaining eight features in the core package address system reliability, remote access, and integration with the broader home automation ecosystem.
body.p_35: A background monitor that detects application freezes and triggers automatic restart. The watchdog preserves session state across restarts, so the session resumes from the last auto-save after a UI crash.
body.p_36: Multi-machine architecture allows remote monitoring from any device with a web browser. The laptop next to the mount handles hardware communication; a desktop across the house provides the control interface. Both stay synchronized via WebSocket state replication.
body.p_37: Real-time status display — mount position, camera state, weather, guiding error, stacking progress — served from the local machine. No installation required on the viewing device. Works on phones, tablets, and laptops.
body.p_38: Every session is recorded: target coordinates, exposure times, guiding metrics, weather conditions, and user actions. The database is fully searchable, enabling historical analysis of tracking performance across months of data.
body.p_39: Observatory state is published to an MQTT broker for home automation integration. Node-RED, Home Assistant, and custom scripts can subscribe to mount position, session status, and safety alerts.
body.p_40: Over 60 endpoints expose the main subsystems. The API is documented, versioned, and supports both JSON and message-pack serialization. Custom frontends, mobile apps, and third-party tools can control the observatory without using the HYBRID UI.
body.p_41: The final four features target users who operate multi-equipment setups and need structured configuration and data management.
body.p_42: Saved configurations for telescope, camera, mount, and filter wheel combinations. Switching between a wide-field refractor setup and a deep-sky SCT rig takes one click instead of reconfiguring every parameter manually.
body.p_43: Two weather data sources — OpenWeatherMap for general conditions and Meteoblue for astronomical seeing forecasts. Both are polled at configurable intervals, and the data feeds directly into the safety monitor and scheduler.
body.p_44: The daemon, web, and desktop components can run on separate machines. The daemon handles hardware communication on the mount-side laptop. The web dashboard runs on any device. The desktop app provides the full Electron interface on a control room machine. State synchronization between them is automatic.
body.p_45: Full session data export in JSON format. Import previous sessions for comparison, reproduce imaging runs, or transfer configurations to a new machine. The export includes target metadata, exposure sequences, guiding logs, and weather records.
body.pull_quote_38: HYBRID combines voice control, predictive ML tracking, cloud observatory access, and dome automation in a single package that runs on a laptop next to the mount.

article.headline: Six-Phase Code Audit: 83 Findings, 10 Fixes, 1,495 Tests Passing
article.deck: A systematic six-phase audit of the entire HYBRID codebase — 83 issues found, 10 real fixes applied, 8 false positives dismissed, two specifications written for future work, and all tests passing.

sidebar.stat_desc: 429 C# tests + 1,066 Python tests. Each fix was reviewed in a separate agent-based check and followed by a full test-suite run.

body.h2_1: Phase 1: Compilation Blockers and Critical Bugs
body.h2_8: False Positives: Findings Dismissed After Review
body.quote_1: A synchronous status endpoint holds thread-pool threads while it waits. Each .Wait() occupies a thread, and each occupied thread delays the next request.
body.quote_2: Besides defects, the audit identified tested code that was not connected to the application, such as the mosaic stitcher.
body.p_1: This audit focused on existing code rather than new features. After a period of feature work — Kalman filters, ML tracking layers, voice control, MCP integration, 47 telescope tools — the codebase had grown to over nineteen thousand lines of C# and several thousand lines of Python. The audit examined how the code behaves when something goes wrong: build failures, crashes, deadlocks, data errors and thread-safety problems.
body.p_2: We ran a six-phase deep audit: compilation blockers and critical bugs first, then crash and deadlock analysis, data integrity, thread safety, full test verification, and finally a review of incomplete features. Five separate audit agents reviewed the source files, public APIs, threading patterns and error paths. They reported 83 potential issues. Ten were confirmed defects. Eight were false positives. The remaining 65 were lower-priority items that do not affect correctness or stability.
body.p_3: The audit started with bugs that prevent the application from building. A duplicate class name — CatalogStar defined in both the catalog query engine and the photometric color calibration module — caused a compilation failure. The fix was to rename the PCC-specific class to PCCStar and update all six reference sites.
body.p_4: Next, a pair of XMath.Min calls in the GPU stacking kernels could produce negative array sizes under edge conditions. Math.Max(0, ...) guards were added at three locations so the stack size is never negative. The GPU memory manager, meanwhile, was reserving memory blocks without a corresponding cleanup path. We wired MemoryManager.Reserve() and MemoryManager.Free() into all five stacking methods with proper try/finally blocks — the same pattern used in database connection pooling.
body.p_5: The largest change in this phase was to the web server status endpoint. It was using Func<JObject> — a synchronous delegate — to gather telescope position, tracking state, weather data, and scheduler progress. This meant the HTTP response blocked every other request while it collected all that data. We changed it to Func<Task<JObject>>, replaced eight blocking .Wait() calls with await Task.WhenAny for timeout protection, and batched independent queries with Task.WhenAll. In testing, the endpoint now responds in milliseconds rather than seconds.
body.p_6: The second phase looked for bugs that appear mainly under load: race conditions, deadlocks, and unvalidated external input. The Whisper voice engine had a race condition in its TTS process lifecycle. When the Exited event fired, it wrote to _speakingEndTime and _isSpeaking outside the ttsLock that protected them everywhere else. Two threads could see inconsistent state: one thinking speech was still active, the other recording an end time in the past. The fix moves those three lines inside the existing lock, so the speaking state is always read and written consistently.
body.p_7: The catalog query engine accepted user-supplied object names and passed them directly into ADQL queries against the CDS VizieR service. A name like M31'; DROP TABLE stars;-- would not cause data loss (VizieR uses parameterized queries), but it could trigger error messages that confuse users or leak internal details. We added a whitelist regex (^[a-zA-Z0-9\s\-\.\(\)\+\/]+$), a 100-character length limit, and null-check gating. The input is validated before it is sent over the network.
body.p_8: Three issues flagged in this phase were false positives. Each was checked against the code before being dismissed. The autofocus engine was reported as leaking resources, but it already implements IDisposable with proper cleanup in a try/catch. The imaging sequence engine was flagged for missing disposal, but it already has a complete Dispose() method. The Python photometry module was reported as having division-by-zero risks, but every division was already guarded with if > 0 checks. The audit was set up to flag anything that looked suspicious; these items were then checked against the code and closed.
body.p_9: The confirmed defects in this phase were smaller in scope. The noise reduction module was converting floating-point pixel values to 16-bit integers using truncation: (ushort)(value * 65535). This introduces a systematic bias — every pixel is rounded down, and the maximum error is a full quantization step (1/65535). Switching to Math.Round halves the maximum error to 0.5/65535 and eliminates the directional bias. In a noise reduction algorithm, a directional bias matters because it can create artificial gradients that the algorithm then tries to “correct.”
body.p_10: The Claude voice bridge shutdown was sending an empty string instead of the expected STOP command. The Python bridge process would not recognize the empty string as a shutdown signal, leaving it running until the 2-second WaitForExit timeout expired and Kill() was called. The fix: change WriteLine("") to WriteLine("STOP"). The bridge now exits on the command instead of being terminated after the two-second timeout at the end of each voice session.
body.p_11: The voice command counters — voiceCommandsSuccess, voiceCommandsError, voiceCommandsBlocked, and voiceCommandsTotal — were plain int fields incremented with ++ from background threads. The ++ operator is not atomic: it reads the current value, adds one, and writes it back. Two threads can interleave their reads and writes, causing a lost increment. With voice commands arriving every few seconds from the Whisper engine, lost increments could occur in normal use and make the counters inaccurate.
body.p_12: We replaced all 100+ occurrences of voiceCommands*++ with Interlocked.Increment(ref voiceCommands*) across two files. On .NET, Interlocked performs the read-modify-write as a single atomic operation, so concurrent increments are not lost. The rolling confidence tracker (voiceConfidenceSum and voiceConfidenceCount) was also moved inside the existing voiceHistoryLock block.
body.p_13: Four other thread-safety findings were dismissed after investigation. The AutofocusEngine uses CancellationToken rather than a volatile flag — the recommended pattern. The MosaicStitcher’s Parallel.For iterates over rows within a single panel, and each row writes to unique output indices — no cross-thread writes. The CosmeticCorrectionManager is stateless with only readonly fields. And the AutoRunScheduler does not exist in the codebase.
body.p_14: After all fixes were applied, we ran every test suite in the project. The C# test projects — Camera (34 tests), ImageProcessing (384 tests), and Imaging (11 tests) — all passed. The Python voice parser passed all 75 of its tests, and the larger parser suite ran 991 tests covering the Messier, NGC, Caldwell and Collinder catalogues, bright stars, and edge cases in the number parser. Total: 1,495 tests, zero failures.
body.p_15: The build compiled cleanly: zero errors and zero warnings across all projects (Shared, Core, Weather, Camera, ImageProcessing, Imaging, GUI). The 26 tests marked as “ignored” require specific GPU hardware and were correctly excluded from the run.
body.p_16: The final phase asked: what did we build but never wire up? The answer was the mosaic stitching pipeline. MosaicStitcher.cs — 372 lines of tested image assembly code — was not called anywhere. After the MosaicExecutionEngine captured panels and saved them as separate FITS files, nothing assembled them into a final mosaic. The user had to open external software (Siril, PixInsight) to combine the panels.
body.p_17: We added an AutoStitchMosaicPanelsAsync() method that runs automatically when all mosaic panels complete successfully. It recursively searches for FITS files under each panel’s save path, loads them via ImageLoader, computes pixel offsets from the grid layout, calls MosaicStitcher.Stitch() with linear feathering, and saves the result as a 32-bit float FITS file. The wiring was verified end-to-end: the event handler, the file discovery, the image loading, the offset computation, the stitching, and the output.
body.p_18: For the remaining two incomplete features — multi-band cross-filter alignment and ML-based star removal — we wrote formal specifications rather than half-implemented code. SPEC-017 defines differential chromatic refraction correction, per-filter reference frame selection, and filter-aware star detection. SPEC-018 defines an ONNX-based U-Net star removal model with a training pipeline, GUI integration, and star mask generation. Both specs are ready for implementation when the priority warrants it.
body.p_19: Eight findings were dismissed after deeper analysis. The H8 shell injection flag was wrong: Python uses subprocess.Popen(cmd) with a list, not a string, and shell=True is never used. The H9 autofocus leak was wrong: the engine uses delegates and FITS cleanup is in a try/catch. The H10 IDisposable flag was wrong: the class already implements IDisposable. The H13 division-by-zero was wrong: all divisions are guarded. Four thread-safety flags were wrong: the autofocus uses CancellationToken, the mosaic Parallel.For is per-row, the cosmetic correction manager is stateless, and the AutoRunScheduler does not exist.
body.p_20: Dismissing a false positive is not the same as ignoring it. Each one was verified by reading the actual code, tracing the control flow, and confirming the safety property. The audit was set to flag too much rather than too little, and the verification phase was designed to catch exactly this kind of over-reporting.
body.p_21: The 1,495 tests were used both to check the fixes and to detect regressions. Every change was made, committed, and re-tested before the next phase started. The reported test count went from 366 (after the roadmap sprint) to 1,495, mainly because all test projects are now included in the count. No existing test changed its result.
body.p_22: Of 83 flagged issues, 10 were confirmed defects (about 12%), 8 were false positives and 65 were lower-priority items. A high proportion of non-defects is expected from an audit configured to flag anything suspicious; the cost is the time needed to verify each flag against the code.
body.p_23: The mosaic stitching engine had 372 lines of tested code and six passing unit tests. It was not called from anywhere in the application. The fix was not a bug patch but an integration change: mosaic panels are now assembled automatically after capture.

article.headline: Security and Crash Fixes: 15 Critical and High-Severity Issues Across 12 Files
article.deck: A five-agent audit of the codebase produced 135 findings. This pass fixed 15 CRITICAL and HIGH-severity issues — hardcoded secrets, division-by-zero crashes, UI deadlocks, memory leaks, and incorrect build paths.

sidebar.title: Audit in Numbers
sidebar.stat_desc: 16 CRITICAL, 39 HIGH, 36 MEDIUM, 25 LOW. 15 CRITICAL and HIGH fixes applied in this pass; the remaining items are recorded in the fix log.

body.p_1: Some defects produce no error messages or stack traces in normal use. Examples from this audit: a signing key stored in an XML file, a division that works at mid latitudes but fails at the poles, and a synchronous wait that deadlocks only under particular timing. Code of this kind can pass the existing tests because the tests do not exercise the edge case.
body.p_2: After the first audit (Fixes 1–18, July 2026), a second audit ran five parallel agents — one for C# GUI, one for C++ native code, one for Python STT services, one for build and configuration, and one for the MCP server and tests. They reported 135 new findings. Sixteen were CRITICAL. Thirty-nine were HIGH. The rest were lower-priority items. This article describes the 15 CRITICAL and HIGH fixes applied in this pass, and the conditions under which each defect appeared.
body.p_3: The HMAC signing key used to validate license keys was sitting in App.config in plaintext: HYBRID_TELESCOPE_CONTROL_2026_SECRET_KEY_V1. Anyone with a copy of the source code — or a decompiled binary — could generate valid license keys for any machine. The LicenseManager.cs file had a fallback constant that returned this key when no environment variable was set, which was always.
body.p_4: We removed the hardcoded value from both the config file and the C# constant. GetHmacKey() now throws InvalidOperationException if neither the HYBRID_LICENSE_HMAC_KEY environment variable nor the App.config entry is present. This is a breaking change for any installation that relied on the default; that is intentional.
body.quote_1: A default signing key would be the same key in every installation. With the fallback removed, a key must be configured before licence validation runs.
body.h2_2: Fix 25: Division by Zero at the Poles
body.p_5: The AltAzToRaDec function in MathUtils.cpp divides by cos(dec) when computing hour angle. At the celestial poles, declination reaches plus or minus 90 degrees, and cos(90°) is zero. The resulting NaN propagates through the coordinate pipeline into telescope motor commands, causing erratic pointing near the poles — a case the tests, which all ran at latitude 45°N, did not cover.
body.p_6: The fix: an epsilon guard. If the absolute value of cos(dec) is below 10−10, the hour angle defaults to zero (the local sidereal time). The Haversine distance function had a similar issue: its intermediate variable a could exceed 1.0 due to floating-point imprecision, making sqrt(1-a) a square root of a negative number. We clamped a to [0, 1] before the square root.
body.p_7: Six call sites in MainWindow.Imaging.cs were using .GetAwaiter().GetResult() to synchronously wait for async ASCOM HTTP calls. On the WPF UI thread, this can deadlock: the async continuation tries to post back to the SynchronizationContext, which is blocked by the synchronous wait. The deadlock would manifest only under specific timing conditions — when the ASCOM response arrived while the UI thread was still processing — which makes it difficult to reproduce in testing.
body.p_8: We wrapped all six call sites in Task.Run(() => ...), which moves the async work to the thread pool and prevents the SynchronizationContext capture. This is the standard WPF pattern for breaking sync-over-async deadlocks.
body.p_9: ASCOMControllerWrapper.Dispose() called DisconnectAsync().Wait(2 seconds). If Dispose was called from the UI thread (which it is, during window shutdown), the same SynchronizationContext deadlock would occur. The fix: wrap in Task.Run() so the async disconnect runs on the thread pool while Dispose returns immediately.
body.p_10: The MCP SSE proxy in WebServer.cs created a MemoryStream for each incoming request body but never disposed it. Over hours of continuous operation, the undisposed streams accumulated. The fix was one line: using (var bodyStream = new MemoryStream()). The using block ensures disposal even if the method throws.
body.p_11: The shared HttpClient for MCP proxy requests had a 24-hour timeout. A hung connection would block a thread pool slot for an entire day. It is now 5 minutes, which is long enough for SSE streams and short enough to avoid holding thread-pool slots indefinitely.
body.p_12: Six HIGH-severity issues were in build configuration rather than runtime code:
body.li_1: Fix 22 (.gitignore): EXTRA PROGRAMS/ and GENERATE LICENCE KEYS/ were at root level in .gitignore but the actual directories were under extras/. The license key generator and 400+ MB of installer executables were tracked in git.
body.li_2: Fix 23 (Deploy scripts): Server IP 192.168.1.55 and SSH username christm45 were hardcoded in deploy-all.bat. Replaced with environment variables HYBRID_VM_IP and HYBRID_VM_USER.
body.li_3: Fix 24 (.vscode/mcp.json): All paths were hardcoded to C:\Users\Bogdan\Desktop\release\.... Replaced with ${workspaceFolder} variables.
body.li_4: Fix 33 (.csproj): The TelescopeMCP Exists() condition checked ..\TelescopeMCP\dist\ while the Include used ..\tools\TelescopeMCP\dist\. The condition always failed, so the MCP server was never copied to build output.
body.li_5: Fix 34 (NSIS): The installer referenced download_whisper_mic.py but the actual file is download_whisper_model.py.
body.li_6: Fix 35 (OxyPlot): ImageProcessing referenced OxyPlot.Wpf 2.1.2 while GUI referenced 2.2.0, risking TypeLoadException at runtime.
body.p_13: SimpleJSON.h’s value parser used find('"') to locate the closing quote of a JSON value. If the value contained an escaped quote (\"), the parser would match the backslash-escaped quote and truncate the value. We replaced the plain find() with a loop that skips escape sequences.
body.p_14: ConfigManager.cpp’s WriteFile() did not check whether the write actually succeeded. On disk-full or I/O error, it returned true, and the caller assumed the config was saved. Next load would read stale or empty data. We added file.flush() plus a file.fail() check.
body.p_15: After all 15 fixes were applied, we ran a clean rebuild of the entire solution. All 12 projects compiled with zero errors. The output binary HYBRID_Telescope_Control.exe is 9.2 MB. Each change was also reviewed by re-reading the modified code.
body.card_p_1: 15 CRITICAL and HIGH fixes across 12 files. Security, crashes, deadlocks, memory leaks, data corruption, and build configuration.
body.card_p_2: The existing test suites pass, including the 1,495 tests from Phase 5 (of which 1,066 are Python tests). No regressions were observed.
body.p_16: The audit reported 135 issues. This pass applied 15 fixes to CRITICAL and HIGH-severity findings. The 61 MEDIUM and LOW items are documented in the fix log. They include empty catch blocks that swallow errors, data races in non-critical paths, async methods without await, date-dependent test cases, and various cosmetic issues. They will be addressed when those files are next changed.
body.p_17: The scope of this pass was limited to issues that could cause crashes, deadlocks, resource leaks or security exposure. Lower-severity items were deferred.

article.headline: Six Requested Features: Cometary Tracking to Spectroscopic Slit Alignment
article.deck: An observer listed six capabilities that were not yet in the feature list. This article describes the engine-level implementation of each, the tests that cover it, and the hardware integration that is still pending.

sidebar.title: By the Numbers
sidebar.stat_desc: Six features, sixty-seven new tests, no regressions in the existing suite. Each feature was implemented, run through the full suite, and logged before the next one was started.

body.p_1: The request came in plain terms. An observer went through the capability list and pointed at six gaps: cometary offset tracking, real multi-camera and camera-to-mount synchronization, hierarchical dynamic scheduling, spectroscopic slit alignment, full ASCOM Alpaca support for the safety and weather devices, and a remote scheduling interface. “I hope you can tell me when and if these will be coming along.”
body.p_2: This release implements the core of all six: the math and the control logic, each covered by tests that run on every build. It does not yet include end-to-end integration with the user interface and live hardware. The work that still needs a real mount and camera on the bench is listed at the end of each section.
body.h2_1: 1. Cometary Tracking and ASCOM Rate Units
body.p_3: Comets, asteroids and the Moon drift against the fixed stars, so a mount tracking at the sidereal rate slowly leaves them behind. ASCOM solves this with two offset rates added on top of sidereal — and their units are a common source of errors. DeclinationRate is arcseconds per SI second, straightforward. RightAscensionRate is seconds of right ascension per sidereal second, which is not the same second, and is a coordinate measure rather than an on-sky one.
body.p_4: The new converter takes rates the way observers actually receive them — the “dRA·cosD” and “dDEC” columns off a JPL Horizons or Minor Planet Center ephemeris — and turns them into the exact units the mount expects: divide the RA-coordinate rate by fifteen to go from arcseconds to seconds of time, then multiply by 0.9972695677 to convert an SI second into a sidereal one. It un-projects the on-sky RA rate by cos(Dec), stays finite at the pole, and handles the wrap across the 0h/24h boundary. It can also difference two ephemeris positions directly if that's all you have.
body.quote_1: Fifteen arcseconds per second is exactly one second of RA per SI second — and 0.9972695677 of that per sidereal second. An error in either constant accumulates as a tracking drift, and the comet leaves the frame within minutes.
body.p_5: Left to wire: a voice/UI entry point and an optional built-in orbital-element resolver so rates can come from a designation instead of a pasted ephemeris. The mount now has the required rate methods, and eleven tests cover the conversion.
body.p_6: The application already treated an imaging camera and a guide camera interchangeably, but it did not coordinate them. Two components add that coordination. The first aligns exposure midpoints rather than starts: when a 300-second frame on the main scope and a 60-second frame on a piggyback need to capture the same instant, you center both on a shared midpoint, not a shared start. The second is a per-mount barrier that refuses to let a mount dither or slew while any camera riding it is still integrating. It treats each mount independently, so a two-rig setup dithers each side the moment its own sensors go idle.
body.p_7: Left to wire: binding the channels to live camera and mount instances. The planner and the barrier are pure logic, covered by ten tests.
body.h2_3: 3. Scheduling That Groups the Way Observers Think
body.p_8: The existing scheduler was already dynamic — it re-scored targets by priority and altitude every cycle. It did not support grouping work into projects with shared, inherited rules. The new layer sits on top without touching the flat engine: a project tree where priority is inherited as a maximum (a Critical project lifts everything beneath it, and an individually critical target survives a low-priority project), and constraints combine with the stricter one winning (altitude floors rise, time windows intersect). A flat session is simply a one-project tree, so nothing that worked before changes.
body.p_9: Left to wire: letting the engine consume the tree directly and a tree editor in the UI. Flattening, inheritance and selection are covered by twelve tests.
body.p_10: The web server could already poke the scheduler with ad-hoc commands, but there was no queue with identity. Now there is: a thread-safe job queue where a phone, a broker, or another observatory can submit an observation request, get an id back, and then list, cancel, or reprioritize it while the local scheduler drains the queue by claiming the next-best job — highest priority first, then first-come. Every read returns a copy, so callers cannot modify the queue's internal state, and a test with two hundred concurrent submissions checks that the ids stay unique.
body.p_11: Left to wire: the thin REST endpoints behind the existing session auth, and a drain loop in the scheduler. The queue itself is covered by thirteen tests.
body.h2_5: 5. The Whole Weather Station, Not One Number
body.p_12: Support for the ASCOM safety monitor — the single “is it safe right now” boolean — was already complete. Its sibling device, ObservingConditions, was being read for exactly one value: sky quality. That is now the whole device: temperature, humidity, pressure, dew point, cloud cover, rain rate, wind speed, gust and direction, sky brightness and temperature, and seeing. Each sensor is read tolerantly, because most real stations implement only a subset and ASCOM reports the rest as an error rather than a value — so an absent sensor becomes a blank, never a crash. A pure evaluator turns the readings into a safe/unsafe verdict with plain-language reasons, using one rule: a limit is only evaluated when its sensor reports a value.
body.p_13: Left to wire: pointing the existing sky-quality read at the new client and surfacing the full panel. Client and evaluator carry ten tests.
body.h2_6: 6. Putting a Star on a Slit
body.p_14: Spectroscopy needs the target walked onto a narrow slit and held there, and the control problem is the same shape as autoguiding. Measure the star on the slit-viewer, compute the perpendicular distance to the slit line — only the across-slit component matters, position along the slit is free — rotate that pixel error by the camera angle and scale it by the plate scale to get an on-sky nudge, apply a fraction of it, and repeat. The controller converges under a proportional gain, and it stops and reports failure if the mount does not respond, instead of looping indefinitely.
body.p_15: Left to wire: feeding it real centroids from the slit-viewer and driving the mount's small-offset path. The geometry and the controller are covered by eleven tests.
body.p_16: Each of the six sections above ends with a list of pending work. The engine — the part that has to be numerically correct and can be checked without a telescope — is implemented and tested. Integration with the nineteen-thousand-line main window, the voice grammar, and the live ASCOM devices is recorded as pending. It will be marked complete after it has been tested against real hardware on the bench.
body.p_17: Six features, sixty-seven new tests, and a full suite that went from 299 to 366 with no change in the result of any existing test:
body.p_18: A roadmap date is an estimate. A tested engine layer with its remaining integration work itemized can be inspected directly. For these six requests, that form of answer was also quicker to produce.
body.h3_2: Units Are a Feature, Not a Footnote
body.p_19: The most error-prone line in the batch was a unit conversion — sidereal seconds and seconds of RA in the cometary rate. It has its own test with a hand-computed expected value, because a small error that is invisible in a quick check becomes visible over an hour of tracking.
body.h3_3: A Pure Core Is a Testable Core
body.p_20: Everything here was written as side-effect-free logic first — no HTTP, no camera, no mount — and wired second. As a result, the sixty-seven tests run in under two seconds and can catch errors before any hardware is involved.

article.headline: Disk-Banded Stacking: A 564-Frame Session in About 1 GB of RAM
article.deck: A 564-frame session required 26 GB of RAM and was refused by the memory check. The stacker now reads horizontal bands from disk, which brings memory use to about 1 GB, and the resulting master is identical to the whole-frame result pixel for pixel. The work also found that three default settings routed sessions back to the old path, and that drizzle had been disabled for years because it was never given the dither offsets.

sidebar.title: One Real Session
sidebar.stat_label: 563 of 564 frames stacked, calibrated and normalized
sidebar.stat_desc: 4144×2822 each, on a machine that previously refused the job. Peak working set: roughly 780 MB. The frame that did not make it was cut in half by an interrupted capture, and is excluded on purpose.

body.p_1: The bug report was one sentence: loading 500 frames and pressing STACK gives “Stacking cancelled — not enough memory, 43 GB needed.”
body.p_2: The memory guard was right. Every frame was being held as a float[] for the entire duration of the run. Five hundred frames of 4144×2822 is 21.8 GB before anything else happens, and alignment doubles it while it builds the warped copy. The guard was doing its job. The pipeline behind it was the problem.
body.p_3: Nothing about combining images requires all of them at once. Stacking is a per-pixel operation: to produce row 900 of the master you need row 900 of every frame, and nothing else. The new stacker is built on that property.
body.p_4: The stacker now walks the image in horizontal bands, seeking each frame’s rows straight off the disk and combining them with the same per-pixel code the old path used. A 500-frame session holds about 1 GB regardless of frame count, against 21.8 GB resident before.
body.p_5: The design requirement was that the banded path must produce the same result as the whole-frame path. If reading from disk produced a slightly different master, the result would depend on how much RAM was free — a form of non-determinism that is hard to reproduce on a different machine. So the tests assert equality with zero tolerance, band by band, against the whole-frame result.
body.p_6: The zero-tolerance tests found a difference early. The decode path had to reproduce the whole-frame conversion exactly, including a (ushort) truncation that happens before dividing by 65535. Rounding instead — which is arguably more correct — puts the two paths one ADU apart, and the master would then depend on which code path ran. We kept the truncation and documented why.
body.quote_1: Reading from disk changes memory use, not the result. If the two paths disagreed, the master would depend on the amount of free RAM.
body.p_7: Alignment was the last thing forcing a whole session into memory, and it was the expensive one: it held every frame and built a warped copy beside it. That is where the 43 GB came from.
body.p_8: Alignment, however, consists of two separate steps. Measuring a frame’s transform — detect stars, match the pattern, fit the affine — genuinely needs a whole frame, but only one at a time. Applying that transform is per-band work: an output band is read from a source band, shifted and slanted by the transform, plus the reach of the resampling kernel.
body.p_9: So it is split. Transforms are measured one frame at a time, costing one frame of memory. The warping happens inside the band loop, reading exactly the rows that band needs.
body.p_10: Rotation needs particular care. A shifted band is still a band. A rotated band is a slanted swathe whose height grows with the image width, not the band height. On a 4144-pixel-wide sensor, a fifth of a degree of field rotation adds a dozen rows to every read. That relationship also made it harder to write a regression test that detects the problem than to write the fix — see below.
body.h2_3: Issues Found by Running the Application
body.p_11: All of the above was implemented and its tests passed, but with the default settings the new path was not used.
body.p_12: Launching the application, loading the 564-frame session and pressing STACK produced the same message: “Stacking cancelled — not enough memory.”
body.p_13: The application ships with three settings that each, independently, sent the session back to the old path:
body.card_p_1: On by default above ten frames. GPU stacking needs every frame resident and cannot read from disk at all, so a large session went straight back to being refused. It now yields: when a session does not fit in memory but can be banded, the banded path is used, since it is the route that can complete.
body.card_p_2: Normalization combined with alignment was refused by the banded path. It now measures its factors on the warped frames, at the cost of a second warp in the preliminary pass. Previously the refusal meant the banded path was never used for a default session, which is the case it was designed for.
body.p_14: The third was calibration. A master dark was loaded, as it would be for any real session, and calibration forced whole frames. Yet calibration is per pixel and the masters are single frames: a band of a light needs only the matching band of each master. It bands now, through one shared implementation used by both routes, because two copies of that arithmetic would make the master depend on which route the session took.
body.p_15: The unit tests did not cover the application’s default settings; this was found by launching the executable and running a stack.
body.h2_4: One Bad Frame Refused the Whole Session
body.p_16: With the defaults fixed, the run got further: it measured all 563 transforms, took fifteen minutes doing it — and then declined, falling back to the in-memory path, which refused for memory.
body.p_17: The band buffers were sized by the worst transform in the session. RANSAC had returned one badly rotated frame; that single frame needed a slice most of the image tall, and multiplying its demand by 563 frames exceeded the 1.5 GB budget by a factor of seventeen. A single outlier frame caused the whole session to be refused.
body.p_18: Buffers are sized per frame now. The outlier costs 47 MB — one frame — and the other frames are unaffected. Frames whose alignment demands an outsized slice are reported as a warning, because such a transform is suspect and worth looking at.
body.p_19: Writing the regression test for this took longer than the fix. A rotated band’s extra reach scales with image width, so a narrow test fixture cannot tell per-frame sizing from worst-frame sizing — the rotated frame costs no more than the others and the bug hides. The band also has to be much shorter than the image, as it is in reality. The test was checked in both directions: it passes with the fix and fails without it.
body.quote_2: The per-frame sizing test was run against the old code to confirm that it fails there, and against the fix to confirm that it passes.
body.quote_2_cite: On writing the per-frame sizing test
body.p_20: Drizzle has been in the codebase for years with its checkbox greyed out. The XAML comment beside it stated the reason: StackViaDrizzle handed the drizzle engine null transforms, so every frame was dropped at the same place on the output grid. That produces an upscaled average rather than a drizzle reconstruction, which is why the option was left disabled.
body.p_21: The missing piece was per-frame dither offsets. That is exactly what the new alignment measurement produces.
body.p_22: Drizzle now streams: a frame is dropped onto the output grid and never looked at again, so the natural streaming axis is frames rather than rows. The accumulators are sized by the output — about 750 MB at 2× on this sensor — and do not grow with frame count.
body.p_23: The test that matters compares against a known high-resolution truth: an undersampled synthetic scene, sixteen frames dithered by quarter pixels, drizzled 2×. The result must be closer to the truth than the same frames stripped of their offsets, which is the old behaviour. On this test its RMS error is 50 percent lower.
body.p_24: Writing that test also caught an error in the test itself before it caught anything in the engine. A frame that samples the scene at +dx must have its pixels placed back at +dx; we had the sign inverted, which doubles the error instead of removing it, and the “dithered” result came out worse than the blind one. The engine was correct; the error was in the test’s measurement.
body.p_25: Three suites were run: 461 imaging tests, 638 GUI tests, 23 imaging-orchestration tests. All pass.
body.p_26: Getting there required fixing a timing-related failure. Two performance benchmarks failed reporting 1,251,245 ms and 1,252,556 ms against a 60-second ceiling. Those numbers are not slow code — they are almost exactly the duration of the entire test run. The assembly executes sixteen test methods in parallel, and those two were starved of CPU for their whole duration while the other tests and a Release build ran.
body.p_27: A wall-clock limit is unreliable when tests share the machine. Marking the benchmarks [DoNotParallelize] took the suite from 21 minutes with two failures to 3 minutes 10 with none. An earlier attempt to fix a similar test with “best of three” had made it worse — every repeat competed too.
body.p_28: Every other test in this area builds its own FITS files, so they share the same assumptions about what a FITS file contains. The pipeline was therefore also run against a real capture: 564 frames of NGC 2903, 4144×2822 RGGB, 23 MB apiece, with the 100-frame master dark the observer actually uses.
body.p_29: Both paths produce an identical master, pixel for pixel — unaligned, and aligned with transforms measured from disk. 563 of 564 frames, in 13 minutes 34, at roughly 780 MB.
body.p_30: The 564th is excluded on purpose. It was cut to 44 percent of its size by an interrupted capture, and is dropped before the run starts with a warning — rather than failing the session partway down the image, which would have stacked the top of the master from more frames than the bottom.
body.p_31: Real data also found something fixtures never could: a band of a real frame is 4 MB, and the band reader allocated a fresh buffer for every read. That is 11,500 large-object-heap allocations over a full session, and the heap climbed to 1.7 GB on a ten-frame run — more than simply loading the frames would have cost, which negated the memory saving. It reads through a reused 64 KB buffer now, below the large-object threshold.
body.h2_8: Corrections to Weighting, Rejection and Reporting
body.p_32: Once stacking ran from disk, quality weighting and “auto-reject worst N percent” were silently ignored: Weight and FrameRejected are derived from the measured statistics rather than copied with them, and the new path never derived them. Every frame came out weighted equally and none was ever dropped.
body.p_33: Separately, “Images stacked” and the SNR estimate counted frames loaded rather than frames combined. A run that discarded the worst 25 percent still reported every frame as used, and overstated the SNR gain to match.
body.p_34: And a smaller one that users see first: an imported session showed every frame rated Poor, in red, before anything had analysed it. The rating was derived from the quality score alone, and an unanalysed frame scores zero. That rating was misleading for frames that had not been measured. There is now a distinct “not analysed” state, shown as a dash in grey; a frame that was measured and came out bad still says Poor.
body.p_35: Two packaging problems affected this release.
body.p_36: The first: running dotnet build silently replaces the executable in the Release output using a toolchain that cannot compile the C++ projects. The result is an .exe from one toolchain sitting beside Core.dll and Shared.dll from another — and the packaging gate checks that those DLLs are present, not that they were built together. We caught it by timestamp: the executable was from 13:10 today, the native DLLs from 21:11 yesterday. The fix is to delete the intermediates and run the master build script, because MSBuild otherwise judges everything up to date and rebuilds nothing.
body.p_37: The second: editing a .bat file with a Unix tool converted its line endings from CRLF to LF, and cmd.exe then mis-parses if/else blocks. The build printed both [OK] HYBRID_Telescope_Control.exe and [ERROR] Executable missing for the same check, showing that both branches had executed.
body.p_38: The installer is 2.62 GiB. Its SHA256 is recorded in version.json, and the deploy verifies the uploaded file against that value on the server before anything old is removed — a guard added after a previous release shipped a silently corrupted upload. We also confirmed that the new archive was created fresh rather than appended to an old one: 7z a updates an existing archive rather than replacing it, which is how a 1.3.4 payload once ended up inside a 1.3.5 installer.
body.p_39: Local (per-tile) normalization still takes the whole-frame path. Comet stacking is not implemented (DeepSkyStacker, for comparison, offers three comet modes). MAD-based rejection variants and noise-weighted stacking, both available in Siril, are not implemented.
body.p_40: One gap remains: the full end-to-end run — measure and stack, aligned, on all 564 frames in one pass through the interface — has not been completed since the last fix. The mechanism is covered by a regression test that fails without it, and the engine has done the work at scale. A complete run through the interface is still to be done.
body.card_p_3: Banded stacking with alignment, calibration and normalization. Drizzle enabled, using measured dither offsets. Nine correctness fixes in the surrounding pipeline. 1,122 tests passing across three suites.
body.card_p_4: The master. Every banded result is verified bit-for-bit against the whole-frame path, on synthetic fixtures and on the real 564-frame session.
body.p_41: The session that previously could not be stacked now stacks in about fourteen minutes on the same machine. The sections above describe the changes required, including one case where the code was correct and the test was wrong.

article.headline: Registration Fix: Stuck Pixels Were Matched as Stars
article.deck: Twenty-nine frames out of thirty-nine came back from registration with the identity transform — reporting a residual of 0.002 px and a quality score of 88 to 94. They had not been aligned. The cause was the order of two steps in star detection, and the 1,298 existing tests, which all passed, did not cover it.

sidebar.title: Before and After
sidebar.stat_label: frames out of 39 returning the identity transform
sidebar.stat_desc: Same session, same forty frames, same entry point. The residual moved from an implausibly low 0.002 px to 0.23–0.35 px, and a separate change made registration 2.3× faster.

body.p_1: This one started as an audit, not a bug report. The questions were broad — is the pipeline correct, are the features connected to the interface, how does stacking compare with Siril and DeepSkyStacker — and the audit answered them by measuring the released binary against real frames rather than by reading code.
body.p_2: The registration engine was run on the first forty lights of a real 569-frame session, and its output was printed. This table led to the fixes in this release:
body.p_3: Frame 37 has moved 37 pixels. Frame 39, two exposures later, reports that nothing moved at all — and reports it with a higher quality score than any frame that was actually registered. That is not consistent with a tracking mount. Twenty-nine of the thirty-nine measurable frames came back this way, every one of them flagged Success = true.
body.pull_quote_1: An RMS of 0.002 px is below what star centroids measured through the atmosphere can achieve. It indicates that the points being fitted are not stars.
body.p_4: The residual is the key indicator, and it runs against the usual expectation that a lower residual is better. Star centroids are fitted from noisy data through an atmosphere. Seeing, photon noise and the fit itself put a floor of roughly a tenth of a pixel on the residual of a correct registration; the healthy session we measured afterwards sits at 0.23 to 0.35 px.
body.p_5: Two-thousandths of a pixel is not a better fit than that. It indicates a different kind of object: the points being matched are in exactly the same place in both frames, to a precision no real measurement of the sky can reach. Something in those frames was not moving.
body.p_6: Printing the detected star list against a raw frame showed the cause. Here is one of the brightest detections, at pixel (1883, 919), in three frames spread across the session:
body.p_7: One pixel at 65,532 — saturated — in a background of about 520. A stuck pixel. And the star detector had it in the top ten, with an amplitude of 7,250.
body.p_8: Five of the ten brightest detections on that frame were defects of the same kind. Measured between the first and twelfth frame, real stars moved about 28 pixels. The defects moved between 0.0005 and 0.002 pixels. A factor of roughly fifteen thousand.
body.p_9: The detector has a hot-pixel filter. It has a saturation filter. Both were enabled. Neither triggered, because of the order in which the steps run.
body.p_10: Raw Bayer data has a two-pixel colour checkerboard that breaks Gaussian PSF fitting, so before fitting anything the detector runs a 3×3 box filter to average it out. That step is reasonable, but everything downstream — the fit, the saturation check, and all five hot-pixel tests — then read the smoothed array.
body.p_11: A 3×3 box filter divides an isolated spike by nine. 65,532 becomes 7,281. The saturation threshold is 60,000, so ExcludeSaturated saw nothing to exclude. And the same smoothing had spread the spike across its neighbours, so the tests that ask “are seven or eight of this pixel’s neighbours dark?” and “is the average neighbour below 30 percent of the centre?” both answered no. By the time it reached the filters, the stuck pixel looked like a star.
body.p_12: The fix is to keep the smoothed array for fitting, which is what it is for, and hand the raw array to the two checks whose entire job is to notice something the smoothing destroys.
body.p_13: Detecting a few extra false stars would normally be a minor quality issue. Here it caused registration to fail, because of one property these false stars have: they never move.
body.p_14: Registration works by finding the set of correspondences that agree on a single transform. Real stars drift together across a session as the mount tracks and the field rotates — but they drift with seeing noise on top, so they agree with each other to a few tenths of a pixel. The stuck pixels agree with each other perfectly, because they are the same sensor coordinates in every exposure.
body.p_15: RANSAC does what it is designed to do: it finds the largest mutually consistent subset. Handed a mix of real stars agreeing to 0.3 px and sensor defects agreeing to 0.002 px, it picks the defects. And the only transform consistent with points that never move is the one that says nothing moved.
body.p_16: So the engine returned the identity, refined it against the survivors, measured a residual of essentially zero, scored that as excellent, and passed it on. Every frame was warped by nothing and stacked as though it had been registered.
body.p_17: This closes an investigation that had been open since 1.3.5, filed as “outer-field signal loss.” Any rejection method destroyed 30 to 90 percent of the signal beyond about 500 px from the centre, while plain Mean stacking looked acceptable. We had ruled out the rejection maths, the stacking loop, the Bayer interaction and the transform model, and had recorded a suspicion about RANSAC that pointed in the right direction but described the wrong mechanism.
body.p_18: The explanation is simpler. Outside the centre the frames were never on top of each other. Mean stacking blurs unregistered frames together and still produces something; rejection looks at a pixel stack containing a star in one frame and background in the next, decides the star is the outlier, and throws it away. The radial pattern came from the target being centred: near the middle the drift is a small fraction of the star profile, out at the corners it is not.
body.p_19: The previous investigation had also run a phase correlation and got zero shift back with a correlation peak of 0.79, which appeared to contradict the misalignment explanation and delayed the investigation by about a week. It is consistent with it. Phase correlation was locking onto the same fixed pattern, for the same reason.
body.p_20: Fixing the detector fixes this instance. It does not fix the class. Any future degeneracy that produces a perfectly self-consistent set of non-stars would fail the same way, and would again be reported as the best frame in the batch.
body.p_21: A registration whose residual falls below 0.01 px is now refused, with an error message explaining that a fit this tight indicates non-stellar points. The check is inexpensive, should not trigger on real star fields, and turns this class of silent failure into a reported error.
body.h2_7: Three More Things Wrong With the Matcher
body.p_22: A closer review of that code found three further problems in the triangle matcher, previously masked by the stuck-pixel bug.
body.p_23: Vertices were labelled by brightness. Triangles were built over indices i < j < k of each frame’s own brightness-sorted star list, then matched vertex-one-to-vertex-one. That is only correct if both frames rank those three stars identically — and seeing, thin cloud and the filters frequently reorder stars of similar brightness. When the ranking differed, the triangle was either missed outright or matched under a permutation, voting three wrong correspondences into the pool. Vertices are now ordered by the shape itself: vertex one sits opposite the longest side. Triangles too close to isosceles to order unambiguously are skipped rather than guessed at.
body.p_24: The hash lookup never probed its neighbours. Triangle shapes are bucketed by truncating two side ratios at 0.01, and matching allows a total error of 0.05. But the lookup only ever examined the exact bucket, so a genuine pair straddling a bucket edge — 0.4999 against 0.5001 — was discarded before the tolerance could be consulted. It now also probes the eight neighbouring buckets, which costs nine dictionary lookups instead of one and lets the tolerance decide.
body.p_25: Two invariants were computed and never read. The triangle angles were calculated on every triangle and then ignored; matching compared side ratios alone. They are part of the test now.
body.p_26: A smaller issue, similar to the settings that bypassed banded stacking in the previous release: MaxStarsForMatching, a configuration property that names this exact stage, was overridden by a hardcoded 30. Thirty stars is a small set; Siril, for comparison, registers on hundreds.
body.p_27: The audit also covered stacking performance. Two changes were made, both measured.
body.p_28: Registration ran frames strictly one at a time on one thread: load, detect, match, next. The disk read of frame n+1 never overlapped the CPU work on frame n. Frames are independent here, so they now measure concurrently — capped at four rather than one per core, because this code path is designed not to hold the session in memory. That took 1.72 seconds per frame down to 0.76: about sixteen minutes of registration on a 564-frame session becomes about seven.
body.p_29: The rejection kernel allocated heavily. Sigma clipping — the default — copied each pixel stack into a List<float>, built a fresh List of survivors on every iteration, and called a median that allocated another copy and fully sorted it. Per pixel. Eleven million times per frame. We measured 2,279 gen-0 collections for two megapixels.
body.p_30: Per-thread scratch buffers and a quickselect median removed all of it:
body.p_31: The checksums are identical to the last digit in all three cases. This follows the same rule as the banded-stacking work: a performance change must not alter the master.
body.p_32: One more, in the same loop: per-frame rejection tallies were being maintained with an Interlocked.Add executed once for every frame on every rejecting pixel. On a 500-frame stack that is billions of contended atomic writes, for a statistic the code’s own comment describes as an even-spread approximation. It accumulates per row now and folds once.
body.h2_9: Why 1,298 Passing Tests Did Not Catch It
body.p_33: The test suite passed throughout. 1,298 passing, nothing meaningfully skipped, no analyser warnings in production code. Meanwhile, three quarters of a real session was being stacked unregistered.
body.p_34: The gap is specific. Every registration test used synthetic star fields. Synthetic frames have no stuck pixels. The condition that breaks the engine could not occur in the fixtures, so the tests could not detect it.
body.p_35: There are now four tests that read real lights. They assert that most frames produce a real transform, that no fit reports an impossibly low residual, that the recovered drift is continuous, and — pinning the root cause rather than its consequence — that no detection stays put while the field moves 28 pixels.
body.p_36: The tests were checked by reverting the fix and re-running them: three of the four fail. That check also found a problem in the first version of the tests. Two of the tests were passing on broken code because the new degeneracy guard was quietly turning the bad frames into skipped frames, and the assertions were counting only the frames that remained. The assertions were corrected so that they fail on the broken build.
body.pull_quote_2: Synthetic star fields contain no stuck pixels, so tests built only on them cannot detect this failure.
body.h2_10: Two Implemented Features Without a User Interface
body.p_37: The audit checked every window and control in the application for unconnected handlers. The result: all 476 event handlers in the XAML resolve, there are no dead interactive controls, and only one help window was orphaned.
body.p_38: But two complete algorithms had no user interface at all. Noise reduction — median, Gaussian and non-local means — was implemented, unit-tested, and called from no line of GUI code anywhere. So was narrowband combine: HOO, SHO, HOS, RGB, LRGB and mono-to-RGB. Both now have a panel in the Post-Processing window.
body.p_39: Narrowband is the more significant of the two. It was reachable, but only through a path that shells out to the embedded Python interpreter — which meant the Hubble palette required a 1.4 GB optional install and failed at runtime without it. The managed implementation, the one with the tests, is what runs now.
body.p_40: Two packaging checks were made strict in this release, both closing paths where a broken build could be released without a warning.
body.p_41: The dotnet CLI cannot compile this project’s two C++ libraries. It reports MSB4278 and MSB4057, and then returns exit code zero because the managed projects succeeded — linking against whatever native DLLs a previous Visual Studio build happened to leave behind.
