That matters more here than it would elsewhere, because the astronomy maths has a managed fallback selected at runtime by whether the native import resolves, and those two implementations have already drifted apart twice: once by 180 degrees of azimuth, once by 0.053 arcseconds of sidereal time. A Release build now refuses to complete without them. Debug still warns, so ordinary managed work is not blocked.
body.p_42: The installer had a similar problem. Its Python processing scripts were staged with NSIS’s /nonfatal flag, so a moved or renamed directory produced an installer that built cleanly and shipped without them. Everything routed through the interpreter then failed on the user’s machine with no signal at build time. The flag is gone from the script globs.
body.p_43: A smaller issue, related to the sidereal-time divergence: mount-model calibration timestamps were being built from hours, minutes and seconds with the milliseconds discarded. Half a second of Earth rotation is 7.5 arcseconds of right ascension, folded into every calibration point the pointing model is then fitted to. A model cannot be more accurate than the clock it was built against.
body.p_44: Two-pass registration with automatic reference-frame selection is still not implemented: the first frame of a session is always the reference, so a session that opens on poor seeing sets the ceiling for the whole stack. It is the next item planned.
body.p_45: Local per-tile normalization still forces the whole-frame path. Spectrophotometric colour calibration remains disabled. Comet registration in the stacker does not exist. Generalised hyperbolic and asinh stretch are not there. Mount backlash is reported as not measured rather than estimated.
body.p_46: One limit on the result above: the frames now register correctly, verified against real data on this machine — but the improvement to the finished master is inferred from the transforms, not yet measured end to end against a re-stacked 564-frame result. The mechanism is covered by tests. The full re-stack has not yet been run.
body.p_47: Saturation and hot-pixel rejection read raw luminance. Degenerate fits refused. Triangle matching repaired on four counts. Registration 2.3× faster, sigma clipping 3.0×. Two unreachable features given a UI. Four real-frame regression tests.
body.p_48: Every stacking result. All three rejection kernels were rewritten for speed and produce checksums identical to the last digit — verified before the change was accepted.
body.p_49: The audit was intended to produce a list of items to review. It found an ordering error in star detection and explained a symptom that had been open since release 1.3.5. As in the previous release, the problem was found by running the application on real data and reading its output. The first indication was not an error message but a quality score of 92 on a frame that had not been aligned.

article.headline: Debayering Added: One-Shot-Colour Sessions Now Stack to a Colour Master
article.deck: For years, HYBRID stacked one-shot-colour sessions as a grey mosaic with the sensor’s checkerboard baked into the noise. Colour output required a debayering stage, a registration approach chosen by measurement, and a fix to the FITS writers, which stored three-channel data incorrectly. The work also addressed a 564-frame session that required 147 GB of memory and a folder scan that counted every FITS file twice.

sidebar.title: Registration Accuracy
sidebar.stat_label: lower registration residual when measured on the raw mosaic
sidebar.stat_desc: 1.13–1.80 px on debayered frames against 0.19–0.25 px on the mosaic. The transform is measured on the mosaic and applied to the colour.

body.p_1: A one-shot-colour camera does not record colour. It records a mosaic: a grid of pixels, each sitting behind a single red, green or blue filter, which software must then combine into a colour image. Until this release, HYBRID did not perform that step. A colour session was stacked as a grey Bayer mosaic, the sensor’s two-pixel checkerboard baked into the noise of every frame. The only route to colour was drizzle in CFA mode, and that requires dithered sub-exposures, which an ordinary imaging session does not have.
body.p_2: Many amateur imagers use colour cameras, so this was a significant gap. This release adds debayering, and the sections below explain why the order of the processing steps matters.
body.p_3: Debayering runs after calibration and before registration, and the reason is the calibration masters. A master dark and a master flat are themselves mosaics: they are per-pixel corrections designed to be applied to raw data. Debayer first and you would be subtracting a mosaic from a smoothed image.
body.p_4: Two reconstructions are offered. Bilinear keeps full resolution and is the default. Superpixel turns each 2×2 Bayer cell into a single pixel — half the width and half the height, and no colour artefacts at all. The mosaic layout is read from each frame’s own BAYERPAT header rather than chosen from a list. The frames of a mono sensor are therefore left untouched whatever the setting, and red and blue cannot be swapped for an entire session by one wrong choice in a drop-down.
body.h2_2: Measure on the Mosaic, Apply to the Colour
body.p_5: The straightforward design registers the debayered frames. Both options were measured on a real session before implementation, and registering the debayered frames gave the larger residual.
body.p_6: That is a residual five to seven times larger. At a typical image scale, 1.13 to 1.80 px is more than a second of arc of smear put into every frame before integration begins. The cause is interpolation: it hands the star detector broader, flatter peaks, and the centroids are less precise even though the detector finds more stars.
body.pull_cite_1: What interpolation does to a star detector
body.p_7: So registration is measured on the raw mosaic and the resulting transform is applied to the colour frames. On five real frames of NGC 2903 the status bar read 28 stars, RMS 0.24 px, quality 98, in line with the earlier mosaic measurements.
body.h2_3: Three-Channel FITS Files Were Written Incorrectly
body.p_8: Every FITS writer in the application declared a three-plane cube in the header and then wrote the pixels interleaved, which is not how a FITS cube is stored. Read back by this program or by any other FITS reader, a three-channel master came back as three scrambled images.
body.p_9: The defect had never appeared, because nothing in the program had ever produced a three-channel file before debayering existed. It would have affected every colour master. It is fixed in all three writers, and the five-frame colour stack was read back plane by plane by an independent Python script to confirm it: three genuinely distinct channels.
body.p_10: A related fault sat in drizzle. Its mode was pinned to Mono, so drizzling a colour session produced an upscaled grey image with no way to ask for anything else. It now switches to CFA mode on its own when the frames are colour.
body.p_11: With colour working, the next issue was memory. A session of 564 frames from an ASI294MC asked for 147 GB of memory, because debayering lived in the whole-frame path and the entire session therefore had to fit in RAM as three-channel images. That is far more than most machines hold, and the application, correctly, refused.
body.p_12: The remedy was to move debayering inside the from-disk banded reader, the same mechanism that had already brought a mono session down from 26 GB to about 1 GB. The same 564 colour frames now stack from disk in about 1.5 GB, and the pixels are identical to those produced by the whole-frame path.
body.p_13: This appeared the first time the STACK button was used on real frames in the application window — a step that earlier audits had noted as not yet done. A folder of five FITS lights imported as ten.
body.p_14: On Windows, a three-character search pattern still matches longer extensions: asking for *.fit returns the .fits files as well, a legacy of the old 8.3 short-name rules. The folder scans asked for *.fits and then for *.fit, and for *.tif and then *.tiff, so every frame in the two commonest formats was added twice. Seven places, in five files, did the same thing.
body.p_15: It was not cosmetic. The doubled count fed the frame counter on screen. It fed the memory pre-check, which costed a 564-frame session as 1,128 frames — most of the way to the refusals that send a session down the whole-frame path. And it fed the stack itself, which combined every frame with an exact copy of itself.
body.p_16: That last point matters for rejection. A duplicated pair of identical values narrows the spread that a sigma-rejection step measures, so the thresholds were being computed from data that could not disagree with itself.
body.p_17: A single scanner now answers the question “which image files does this folder hold?” by matching on the extension a file actually has. Eight tests cover it, including one that checks that Windows still behaves this way, so that the explanation in the code is checked if that behaviour changes.
body.p_18: The same session produced a second finding. After a two-minute stack, the completion dialog announced a processing time of 0.0 seconds. The in-memory stacking route — the one the STACK button uses — was the only path in the engine that never started a stopwatch. Every other path did, which is why no test detected it. The elapsed time is now recorded on every outcome, including a cancelled or failed run.
body.p_19: The release also fixes GPU acceleration, which had not been working: a missing assembly binding made every GPU stack fail and fall back to the CPU, so the GPU option never accelerated anything. It now runs. The normalisation pre-pass shows its progress, every stack is written to the log, and when the from-disk route is declined, the reason is shown in the released build rather than only in a debug window.
body.p_20: Superpixel debayering still forces the whole-frame path, because it halves the frame and a band of the output is not a band of the input. Colour balance is not applied: raw one-shot-colour frames are not white-balanced, and a yellow star really does record more blue than red through a typical sensor, so that belongs to post-processing. Local per-tile normalisation still forces the whole-frame path, spectrophotometric colour calibration remains disabled, and two-pass registration with automatic reference-frame selection is still not implemented.
body.p_21: Debayering after calibration and before registration, bilinear or superpixel, with the pattern read from each frame’s own header. Registration measured on the mosaic. Three FITS writers repaired. Drizzle switches to CFA by itself. Debayering moved into the banded reader. One folder scanner. A stopwatch that starts. GPU stacking that works.
body.p_22: Mono sessions. The stacking mathematics, the rejection methods and the banded reader’s pixels are untouched, and a mono sensor’s frames pass through the debayer stage unchanged.
body.p_23: The stacking algorithms themselves were largely in place. Most of the defects in this release were in the surrounding mechanics: a FITS data layout that did not match its header, a search pattern that matched too many files, and a timer that was not started. Most were found by running the application on real frames.

article.headline: Sky Chart: Seven Defects Fixed and Catalogue Positions Corrected
article.deck: Version 1.4.4 PRO fixes seven defects in the sky chart, including an “Engine: Error” state, unused offline imagery, GOTO by name pointing to the wrong area (M 42 resolved to Sagittarius), a three-point polar alignment reading 180 degrees out and a mirrored horizon profile. It also corrects a J2000/apparent frame mismatch and a Moon position 49 arcminutes off. The catalogues were also compared against Siril, OpenNGC, SIMBAD and JPL DE421; the largest error found was 22.9 degrees, for the star Marfik.

sidebar.title: Largest Catalogue Error
sidebar.stat_label: offset of the catalogued position of Marfik from its reference position
sidebar.stat_desc: Ten bright stars were wrong by degrees, and the rest were rounded to 27 arcseconds. All now carry full J2000 positions with proper motion applied to the date.

body.p_1: Errors in a sky chart are easy to attribute to observing conditions: clouds, seeing, drift or polar alignment. Several defects in HYBRID’s chart and catalogues produced symptoms of this kind, which is why they were not identified earlier.
body.p_2: They are listed below in the order they were found.
body.p_3: The sky chart sometimes reported Engine: Error and left areas of missing deep-sky imagery — or no imagery at all on a machine without internet. The cause was in the Stellarium Web Engine build. Its network error handler calls a helper, withStackSave, that the build does not define. The handler runs on any non-success status, so a 404 from the tile server caused a JavaScript exception instead of a reported failure, and the tile remained marked as loading. The missing definition has been restored.
body.p_4: The requests that triggered the handler came from the shipped star catalogues. Their metadata declared no maximum detail level, so the engine requested tiles beyond those installed. The metadata now declares the levels actually present.
body.h2_2: 3. Installed Sky Survey Imagery Was Never Used
body.p_5: The installer included 1 GB of Digitized Sky Survey imagery, but no request was ever made to it. The chart added the local copy and then the online one; the engine keeps only one image survey, so the second replaced the first and all imagery came from the internet. The chart now uses the online survey when it is reachable, for deep zoom, and the installed copy otherwise. Deep-sky imagery now works offline.
body.h2_3: 4 & 5. GOTO by Name: M 42 Resolved to Sagittarius
body.p_6: A GOTO by name went to the wrong part of the sky whenever the name was resolved from the local catalogue rather than the engine’s own — which, offline, is every object. The coordinates were applied as azimuth and altitude instead of right ascension and declination, so the target also moved as the sky turned. A request for M 42 pointed the chart at Sagittarius. It now points at the Orion Nebula.
body.p_7: A related defect: the chart reported object not found — including aloud, through the voice assistant — for objects it had just centred. This is fixed.
body.p_8: Three-point polar alignment reported a correctly aligned mount as being about 180 degrees out in azimuth, and indicated the wrong direction for the adjustment knobs. The mount’s azimuth and the pole’s azimuth were measured from opposite reference directions.
body.p_9: Because the mismatch combines with sidereal time, the reported error changed through the night. A varying error is easily mistaken for seeing or drift.
body.pull_quote_1: The reported error varied with sidereal time, so it resembled drift rather than a fixed offset.
body.pull_cite_1: Why the defect was not found earlier
body.p_10: Users who polar aligned with this tool should repeat the alignment.
body.p_11: The tracking safety check read the horizon obstruction profile mirrored east to west. An obstruction entered due north was applied due south. Only users with a custom profile were affected; the default profile has the same altitude in every direction, so the error had no visible effect there.
body.p_12: After the chart fixes, the catalogue data was compared against Siril, OpenNGC, SIMBAD and the JPL DE421 ephemeris. The comparison found a number of errors.
body.p_13: Ten bright stars were wrong by degrees — Marfik by 22.9, Alphard by 6.2 — and the rest had been rounded to 27 arcseconds. They now carry full J2000 positions with proper motion applied to the date. Messier positions now come from Siril; M 44 had been 19.5 arcminutes out. Caldwell and Collinder names had been matched to NGC numbers by position, which linked Rosette Nebula to NGC 891, Helix to NGC 7331, and 917 Collinder aliases to the wrong cluster. In all, 223 NGC and IC entries lying more than two arcminutes from OpenNGC were corrected. Stars can now also be found by common or Bayer name, such as Albireo or Mizar.
body.p_14: Two further corrections were made. First, all coordinates exchanged between the chart and the mount are now J2000. They had been in the engine’s apparent frame, which in 2026 differs by about 20 arcminutes, so a Sync from the chart wrote that difference into the mount’s pointing model.
body.p_15: Second, the Moon is now computed from the observer’s site, with parallax. The error was about 49 arcminutes; it is now about 2.
body.p_16: Each defect was at an interface: between the web engine and its host application, between the chart and the mount, or between two azimuth reference conventions. Each component could pass its own tests; the error was in the data passed between them, which unit tests do not usually cover.
body.p_17: Missing engine helper restored. Star-catalogue metadata corrected. Deep-sky imagery available offline. GOTO by name resolved as right ascension and declination. Polar alignment measured from one reference direction. Horizon profile read with the correct orientation. Catalogues corrected against four reference sources. J2000 used throughout between chart and mount. Moon position computed with parallax.
body.p_18: The Stellarium Web Engine itself, the catalogue file formats, and the set of commands sent to the mount. The corrections concern the values sent, not the protocol.
body.p_19: None of these defects caused a crash. They produced small pointing and display errors that resembled observing conditions. For this release the catalogues were checked against external references rather than only for internal consistency.

article.headline: Alt-Az Tracking Corrections by Guide Pulses for Drivers Without Rate Control
article.deck: On a Dobsonian alt-azimuth mount driven by an AstroBridge E4, whose ASCOM driver does not accept a tracking rate, HYBRID’s correction commands switched the driver’s own tracking off. Version 1.4.4 PRO sends corrections as guide pulses instead, adds integral action to the correction loop, and fixes several other alt-az issues found during tests on the real instrument.

sidebar.title: Bench Test
sidebar.stat_label: mean error over six minutes against an injected drift of 33.5″ a minute
sidebar.stat_desc: Measured on the real controller board, driven by the real tracking controller. Not yet measured under a real sky.

body.p_1: A tracking loop has to use commands the mount’s driver actually supports. In this case the driver supported fewer commands than its documentation suggested.
body.p_2: The telescope was a Dobsonian on an alt-azimuth mount, driven by an AstroBridge E4 controller. Its ASCOM driver cannot accept a right-ascension tracking rate, but it does accept guide pulses. HYBRID was sending corrections as MoveAxis commands. On this driver, MoveAxis behaves like the hand-controller arrow keys: it does not adjust tracking, it stops it.
body.p_3: Model tracking starts automatically when the application connects. As a result, connecting HYBRID to the telescope stopped the telescope’s tracking.
body.p_4: Both the open-loop model tracking and the closed-loop plate-solve tracking now correct by guide pulses in right ascension and declination, which the driver adds to its own tracking. Corrections are applied on top of the mount’s motion instead of replacing it.
body.p_5: A second error was found in the same code. Right-ascension pulses are sized, as ASCOM defines them, as a rate of change of right ascension, and corrections had been short by the cosine of the declination. At declination 39 this is 22 per cent. It is fixed.
body.p_6: The loop was then run against the real controller board, on the bench, by the real tracking controller:
body.h2_2: Integral Action Added to the Correction Loop
body.p_7: Until this release the correction servo was purely proportional. Against a constant drift that settles slightly off centre without smearing. An alt-az mount does not present a constant drift: the required rate changes continuously, and a proportional-only loop lags behind a changing demand. That lag shows up as trailing.
body.p_8: Measured against a mount simulator, the lag produced about 10 arcseconds of trailing in a 300-second sub-exposure of a target on the meridian — several pixels at typical image scales. With integral action in the loop, the same measurement gives 0.2 arcseconds, below typical seeing. Equatorial mounts also benefit, to a lesser degree, because the standing offset against a constant drift now decays instead of persisting.
body.pull_quote_1: A proportional-only loop lags behind a continuously changing rate demand; integral action removes that lag.
body.h2_3: Imaging Sequence Stopped After One Frame
body.p_9: On alt-az and fork mounts, an imaging sequence stopped after its first exposure. Automatic meridian flip was on by default, and an alt-az mount reports no pier side, which the flip check treated as an error. Alt-az and fork mounts do not need a meridian flip, so the check is now skipped for them.
body.p_10: Several other alt-az imaging changes were made. Exposures are now capped by field rotation, at about two pixels at the corner of the frame; the cap can be turned off. Derotated frames are written to a separate folder instead of overwriting the raw FITS. The position used for derotation is taken at mid-exposure instead of at the end. Refraction is no longer applied twice when the driver already applies it. Model tracking hands the axes to PHD2 while it guides, and PHD2 guiding is stopped before tracking is turned off — that order previously broke guide pulses.
body.h2_4: Connecting No Longer Moves the Mount
body.p_11: Connecting used to unpark a parked mount and run Find Home every time, then report Telescope moved to home position even when nothing had moved. It now reports the current state and sends no motion commands.
body.p_12: Two related fixes: tracking is switched on before a GOTO, because a conforming driver refuses to slew without it — previously every GOTO after an abort or an emergency stop was refused. A GOTO now also releases its lock as soon as the mount arrives. When a Sync fails, the chart shows the driver’s reason instead of only Sync failed.
body.p_13: The tracking correction loop has been tested against a real mount controller on the bench, but not yet under a real sky. On an alt-az mount without a derotator, field rotation will continue to limit exposure length regardless of tracking accuracy; this is a geometric limit, not a software one.
body.p_14: Corrections by guide pulses, sized as a rate of change of right ascension. Integral action in the loop. No meridian flip on alt-az or fork mounts. Exposures capped by field rotation. Derotated frames kept separate from raw frames. Connecting sends no motion commands. Tracking enabled before a GOTO.
body.p_15: Equatorial mounts whose drivers accept a tracking rate. The pulse path is used only where the driver cannot take a rate but does accept guide pulses.
body.p_16: Most of the issues found on the real telescope were straightforward once observed. A mount that stops tracking on connection is a command-compatibility problem, not a tuning problem, and a simulator that accepts every command does not reproduce it.

article.headline: Status Messages, PHD2 Guiding and Tracking Charts Fixed
article.deck: Version 1.4.6 PRO corrects status messages that did not match the actual state of the system. The interface was tested for a week against simulators and a real PHD2 instance. Fixes include detection of a lost mount connection, guide errors shown in the correct unit, five tracking charts that never drew, and machine-learning screens that showed “Active” whenever tracking was running.

sidebar.title: Connecting to PHD2
sidebar.stat_label: time to connect, before and after removing a byte-order mark
sidebar.stat_desc: A byte-order mark caused PHD2 to reject the first request, and the application then waited for its own timeout on every connection.

body.p_1: Status messages such as Connected, Active or Guiding are relied on by users who do not then check the hardware directly. An incorrect status message can therefore cause more trouble than an error that is reported.
body.p_2: For this release the whole interface was tested for a week against simulators and a real PHD2, with the specific aim of finding messages that did not match the actual state. Most of the issues found were incorrect messages rather than crashes.
body.p_3: If the mount disconnected during a session — unplugged, rebooted, Wi-Fi lost — the application kept showing Disconnect, with frozen coordinates and no message. It now reports Lost contact with the mount, with the reason, within about fifteen seconds. The coordinates are shown as unavailable, and the application reports when the link is restored, or when the driver has restarted and must be reconnected.
body.p_4: Related fixes: Refresh no longer reports Connected for a mount that cannot be reached. A failed connection reports its cause — refused, no answer, unknown host — instead of a generic checklist. The log file no longer receives an error every second: in one test a disconnected mount had produced 430 log lines, and it now produces 13.
body.p_5: Connecting to PHD2 blocked the application for ten seconds on every connection. A byte-order mark at the start of the first request caused PHD2 to reject it, and the application then waited for its own timeout. Without the mark, the connection takes about a tenth of a second.
body.p_6: The existing test server used a standard stream reader, which removes the mark automatically, so the problem was only reproducible with the real PHD2.
body.h2_3: Guide Errors in Pixels, Not Arcseconds
body.p_7: The guide RMS value never changed. The application requested a statistics method that PHD2 does not provide; the RMS is now computed from the guide steps.
body.p_8: In addition, guide errors were labelled as arcseconds although PHD2 reports them in pixels, so every value was understated by the pixel scale — by a factor of 4.3 on a 176 mm refractor setup. They are now converted with PHD2’s own pixel scale, and the unit is displayed. The PHD2 panel also has a new guide-error graph, and the guide star PHD2 is tracking is shown live in the guide-camera feed, with a star lost state.
body.pull_quote_1: PHD2 reports guide errors in pixels; they are now converted with PHD2’s pixel scale and shown with their unit.
body.pull_cite_1: On guide errors that were 4.3 times too small
body.h2_4: Tracking Charts That Did Not Draw
body.p_9: Five of the six tracking charts in the Advanced Features window never displayed data. The plot kept an old, empty model; the time window was 0.12 seconds wide; and the vertical axes were fixed at plus or minus one arcsecond.
body.p_10: The charts now draw. The window also reconnects to the tracking controller when it is recreated, loads data recorded before it was opened, and shows the actual applied corrections and altitude-azimuth errors. The session statistics and the Plate Solve tab, which previously received no data, are now fed by the tracking loop.
body.p_11: The machine-learning screens showed Active whenever tracking was running. They now report whether a model exists, its measured quality, and why it is or is not being applied. Reset now deletes the model.
body.p_12: The training was corrected in four ways. It no longer retrains on every cycle once its buffer is full. It no longer blocks the tracking thread. It now predicts the next step rather than a value that was also provided as an input, which removes a label leak. And it is evaluated on a chronological hold-out instead of a shuffled split, since neighbouring samples in a time series are correlated.
body.h2_6: Mosaic Panel Placement from Shared Stars
body.p_13: Mosaic panels are now placed using the stars they share with neighbouring panels. A flipped or rotated camera, and the field rotation of an alt-az mount, are therefore measured rather than assumed. This fixes the automatic stitch after a mosaic sequence, which now averages several frames per panel and uses the configured overlap, and the mosaic mode of the Stacking window, where panels used to be placed on top of each other. A panel that cannot be matched is reported instead of being stacked in place.
body.p_14: The Mosaic Wizard reads the focal length, pixel size and sensor from the equipment profile and camera, sends the panels in the order of the selected pattern, and warns that rotation turns the grid and not the camera. A Stop button now cancels a sequence or a mosaic, and mosaics work with native ZWO ASI and Canon cameras.
body.p_15: The previous release, 1.4.5, included two related fixes. The application could be started twice: a second instance ran alongside the first, the embedded web server moved to another port, and the MCP server for AI assistants failed at start-up with address already in use, so the assistant integration was unavailable without any message. The installer’s Launch option made an accidental double launch likely. A second launch now reports that the application is already running and exits; the automatic restart after a frozen window still works.
body.p_16: Also in 1.4.5: after connecting a native ZWO ASI camera, such as an ASI120 guide camera, the live-view buttons stayed disabled. Both live views now work with a native ASI camera, and a failure to start the video stream is reported instead of showing a black image.
body.p_17: No machine-learning model has yet been trained under a real sky in this project, so the corrected labelling has been verified by design rather than with real data. PHD2 guiding was tested against PHD2 itself and a simulated guider, not with a real camera. Neither has been validated in the field.
body.p_18: Mount connection monitored and loss reported. PHD2 connects without delay, with a computed RMS and correct units. Tracking charts draw. Machine-learning screens describe the actual model state. Mosaics placed from shared stars. A second launch exits instead of conflicting with the first.
body.p_19: Nothing has been tested under a real sky. This release was checked against simulators and against PHD2 itself, and its release notes state this.
body.p_20: Errors that are reported are usually found and fixed quickly. This release addressed the other kind: incorrect status messages and indicators that give no sign of a problem. The method was to review every message the program can display and check whether it reflects the actual state.

article.headline: Canon EOS 550D Bench Test: Imaging Sequence and RAW Capture Fixes
article.deck: With a Canon EOS 550D connected to a PC, Start Imaging Sequence finished in 25 milliseconds and reported success without taking a picture. Version 1.4.7 PRO fixes that defect and several others found in the same test session, all of which required a real camera to reproduce: wrong RAW quality code, a fixed download timeout, an SDK decoding failure and a recovery dialog that closed the application.

sidebar.title: Sequence Duration
sidebar.stat_label: duration of a sequence that captured nothing and reported success
sidebar.stat_desc: Frames captured: 0. Duration: 00:00:00. Average time per frame: 0.0 s.

body.p_1: The test setup was a Canon EOS 550D, a body commonly used in astrophotography, connected to a PC by USB. No mount was connected and, since the test was run in daytime, there was no sky. This isolates the camera and the software from every other component.
body.p_2: The camera was connected, recognised and configured from the sensor database — 5184×3456 pixels, 4.3 µm. Test capture, live view, and changes of shutter speed and ISO all worked. Start Imaging Sequence was then pressed.
body.p_3: After 25 milliseconds the program reported that the sequence had completed successfully. No exposure had been taken.
body.p_4: Neither the activity log nor the window showed any error. A listener was attached to the program’s debug output and the sequence was run again. The engine output was:
body.p_5: A sequence without a per-filter plan runs on an implicit entry named “L”, position −1. The engine sent that entry to the filter wheel like any other. With no wheel connected — the case for every DSLR and most ASI setups — the window’s handler returns false. The engine does not expose a frame through a filter it could not select, since the file would be labelled with the wrong filter, so it skipped the frame.
body.p_6: A second defect followed. The engine stops a run after five consecutive failed frames. The test requested three frames, so three skips stayed under the limit, the loop reached its end, and the result was Success: true, 0 frames.
body.p_7: Both are fixed. The engine now uses the filter wheel only when a filter plan exists, and a run that captured no frames is reported as failed, with its reason.
body.pull_quote_1: Skipped frames were not counted as failures of the run, so a sequence with zero frames was reported as successful.
body.p_8: The next run also stopped immediately, for a different reason. With no mount connected, the meridian-flip check returned unknown, and the engine treats unknown as a reason to abort “to protect the telescope”. With only a camera connected, there is no telescope to protect. Now a mount that was never connected means no flip is needed; only a mount that was connected and then lost is treated as unknown.
body.p_9: That abort was also not displayed. The engine reported its end to the window only through its normal exit path; an exception, a validation error or a cancellation inside a capture returned a failed result that the caller did not check. The screen showed nothing and the Start button stayed disabled. Every exit path now reports to the window.
body.p_10: Once the sequence ran, the files returned were JPEG. The program requests RAW by setting an image-quality code, and the code was wrong: 0x00640F0F instead of 0x0064FF0F, the value in Canon’s own SDK header. The camera rejected the setting, the rejection was ignored, and a RAW request always produced a JPEG. The code is corrected, and a rejected setting is now logged.
body.p_11: A 35-second bulb exposure took 73 seconds to download. The most likely cause is the camera’s long-exposure noise reduction: after a long exposure, the 550D can record a dark frame of the same length before sending the image.
body.p_12: The program waited a fixed 60 seconds for the image, so any exposure longer than about a minute would have lost its picture. The wait now scales with the exposure, and the estimated sequence duration includes the dark frame: 35 seconds is estimated at about 80 rather than 45, against the 73 measured. With noise reduction disabled on the body, the estimate is slightly high, which is the safer direction.
body.p_13: For focus measurement and plate solving, the program must read the camera’s RAW file. Canon’s SDK rejected every attempt to develop the 550D’s file at full size — error 7, not supported, in every output format tried — while decoding the 160×120 thumbnail without error. The cause was not determined.
body.p_14: Every Canon RAW file also contains a full-size JPEG preview. The program now falls back to that preview: eight bits instead of fourteen, which is sufficient for a focus metric or a plate solve.
body.p_15: One defect was unrelated to cameras. After a forced close, the next start shows Interrupted Session Detected. Pressing either Resume or Start Fresh then closed the whole application.
body.p_16: The cause is a framework rule. The application is configured to exit when its main window closes, and the first window created is treated as the main window. The recovery dialog was created first, so closing it ended the program. The dialog is now managed explicitly and is no longer treated as the main window once it has returned its answer.
body.p_17: The live view on the Tracking tab was paced by the shutter speed, giving 0.8 images a second at a one-second exposure, whereas the camera’s own stream delivers about six. It was labelled as an ASCOM camera, and its footer kept showing the camera name after Disconnect. The Cancel button of the camera-type chooser was cut off at the bottom of its window. All four are fixed.
body.p_18: There were no stars in the test images. The frame-quality scorer gives a score of zero to an image without stars, so it requested each frame twice; and the debug build used for the test has no embedded Python, which the scorer requires. A test under a real sky, with a focuser and a mount, is still pending. The 500D, 600D and 700D bodies are untested, and the installer has not yet been run on a clean machine.
body.p_19: The filter wheel is used only when a filter plan exists. A run with no frames is reported as failed. No mount means no flip is required. Every exit path of the engine reports. RAW requests return RAW. The download wait scales with exposure and the estimate includes the dark frame. JPEG preview fallback when the SDK cannot develop the RAW. The recovery dialog no longer closes the program.
body.p_20: A sequence that has a real filter plan still skips a frame when its wheel fails, and stacking results are unchanged. The new engine tests fail on the old code and pass on the new, and the full test suites pass.
body.p_21: Automated tests did not detect that the sequence button produced no exposures, or that the camera was being sent the wrong image-quality code. A real camera connected to the PC reproduced both within the first test session.

article.headline: Unanswered Mount and Accessory Queries No Longer Treated as Completion
article.deck: A session log showed “Slew completed” for a slew that had just been aborted. The cause, found in many places in the code, was that a mount which did not answer a status query was treated as a mount that had arrived. Version 1.4.10 PRO fixes this for the mount and for the focuser, rotator, filter wheel, dome and flat panel.

sidebar.title: Slew-Status Call Sites
sidebar.stat_label: call sites that ask whether the mount is still slewing
sidebar.stat_desc: Most of them treated an unanswered query the same as “no”. The ones that determine the next action — plate solve, sync, flip, imaging — are fixed in 1.4.10.

body.p_1: The scope of this review was the interface, the connections and the settings, with the aim of finding communication errors with the mount and accessories. It started from the log files of real sessions, followed by a reading of the code behind every message that looked incorrect.
body.p_2: One session ended with an abort during a GOTO. Shortly afterwards the log reported that the slew had completed, although the mount had been told to stop. The program then continued as if the mount had arrived: it took an image, plate solved it and synced the mount’s pointing position.
body.p_3: The wait loop asks the mount whether it is still slewing. The answer can be yes, no or nothing, because the link can fail; after two failed attempts the wrapper returns nothing. The loops were written as “keep waiting while the answer is yes”, so nothing ended the wait in the same way as no.
body.p_4: The effect is most serious where it is least visible. A mount that has lost its link is treated as a mount that has arrived. A plate solve then compares the sky with a position the telescope never reached, and a sync writes the difference into the mount as a pointing error.
body.pull_quote_1: An unanswered status query does not indicate that the slew has finished; the mount’s state is unknown.
body.p_5: The mount wrapper now records an abort, and a wait loop that sees one stops with a warning and does not sync. A single unanswered query is tolerated, since drivers occasionally fail to respond; three in a row are treated as a lost link, and the operation stops with that message. The same rule now applies to the scheduler’s slews, its meridian flip, dithering, the re-slew after a sync, the flip on the Imaging tab, Center-and-Rotate, three-point polar alignment and Just-Go.
body.h2_4: Interface Blocked While Waiting for the Mount
body.p_6: Two buttons — the sub-exposure calculator and the start of an imaging sequence — requested the focal length from the mount and blocked the interface thread until it answered. The mount’s timeout is ten seconds, so with an unresponsive mount the window froze for ten seconds per request. These requests are now made without blocking the window.
body.p_7: The same type of defect was found in the accessory code, in three forms.
body.p_8: Timeout reported as success. The focuser waited sixty seconds for a move to finish and then reported Move complete, even when the motor was still running. It now halts the focuser and reports a timeout.
body.p_9: Error read as “finished”. The rotator’s IsMoving returned false when the driver threw an exception, which was interpreted as a completed move. Three failed reads in a row are now an error and the rotator is halted. Its fallback to a second move type, intended for drivers without a mechanical move, also ran on any driver error and could therefore start a second movement; it now runs only when the driver does not implement the method.
body.p_10: Wait ending before motion starts. The filter wheel returned as soon as it saw no motion, which could be before the motion had started. It now waits until the wheel reports the requested slot, and stops waiting promptly if the driver stops responding instead of waiting thirty seconds. The dome’s park and find-home, its shutter, and the flat panel’s cover had the same race condition and now confirm the expected state. A flat panel that never reports ready is now an error, instead of a series of flats being taken with the panel off.
body.p_11: The field derotator read the site latitude and longitude from the mount. When the longitude could not be read, it used zero — Greenwich — without a warning, and rotated the camera on that basis. It now refuses to start and reports why. Stopping the derotator also halts a rotator that is still moving, and the loop warns after five cycles without a position from the mount.
body.p_12: The LX200 driver’s Connect opened the serial port, sent a product query and returned success even if nothing replied, so any open COM port was accepted as a mount. It now fails when the query is not answered, and releases the port.
body.p_13: For the focuser, rotator and filter wheel, a small simulated driver was written. The rotator and filter-wheel tests fail on the old code and pass on the new, covering an unresponsive driver, a move that never ends, and a wheel that reports the old slot. The GOTO loops, the scheduler and the flips are covered by tests that inspect the source code, because exercising them requires a window or a serial port. The full test suite passes.
body.p_14: These tests do not cover the behaviour of a real mount whose link is cut during a slew. The dome and the flat-panel cover have no behavioural tests. The polling timers of the focuser, rotator and filter wheel still read their drivers on the interface thread, because the drivers are created there and moving them is a larger change. A driver that hangs can still freeze the window.
body.p_15: No response from the mount now stops a GOTO, flip, dither or polar alignment instead of completing it. Aborted slews are never synced. Focuser, rotator, filter wheel, dome and cover moves are confirmed or halted. An unreadable longitude stops the derotator. An LX200 that does not answer is not reported as connected.
body.p_16: No test was run on a real mount with its link cut. Polling for three accessories still runs on the interface thread. Stacking, calibration and image results are unchanged.
body.p_17: The program can only act on what the hardware reports. When the hardware does not respond, 1.4.10 now reports the missing response instead of assuming success.

masthead.section_label: Audit • Scheduler • Stacking • after v1.4.11 PRO

article.headline: October Audit, Part 1: Scheduler, Locale and Stacking Fixes
article.deck: Results of a full review of the program’s interface and code by six independent reviewers. Most high-severity findings were not crashes but buttons that reported success without performing their action, and settings that were ignored. This part covers the scheduler, comma-decimal parsing, the pier-side rule, GPU stacking and the remote-access tunnel.

sidebar.title: The Audit in Numbers
sidebar.stat_label: high-severity findings, each checked against the code
sidebar.stat_desc: Six reviewers each took one part of the program: the interface wiring, the mount and tracking, the cameras and sequences, stacking, the web and voice services, and the rest of the interface. All test suites passed before the audit started, which shows that these defects were outside what the tests covered.

body.p_1: The audit covered the whole program, interface and code, with the aim of reporting anything that did not work. Before it began, all test suites passed: 1,016 interface tests and 574 image-processing tests. None of the defects below was detected by them, because almost none raises an error; the affected functions report success.
body.p_2: The Target Scheduler was given the program’s first camera object, which is the guide and plate-solve camera. With a native ZWO or Canon imaging camera, every target failed with “camera not connected”. With an ASCOM guide camera, the light frames were taken through the guide scope. The scheduler also always used bin 1, and a second run on the same evening overwrote the first run’s frames, because the default file name contained no time. The scheduler now uses the imaging camera, applies the configured binning, and does not overwrite existing frames.
body.h2_2: Three Buttons That Did Not Perform Their Action
body.p_3: Apply to Sequence showed “Target schedule applied to imaging sequence!” without reading any targets. RUN PLAN asked for confirmation that “the scheduler will start immediately and run unattended”, then only stored the plan and logged that it was ready. The Night Plan window could not display any plan: one drawing element was added to two parents, which WPF does not allow, so every non-empty plan ended with “Plan generation failed”. An empty schedule was replaced, without notice, by five sample Messier targets.
body.p_4: Apply now passes the schedule to the scheduler queue. RUN PLAN opens the scheduler with the plan’s targets and starts it, after passing it the observing site; an independent review of the fix found that the site was still missing in the first version. The sample targets have been removed.
body.pull_quote_1: Each of these buttons displayed a success message without checking that the action had been carried out.
body.pull_cite_1: On the dialog that applied a schedule it had not read
body.p_5: Windows configured for Serbia, France or Germany uses a comma as the decimal separator. The scheduler parsed right ascension with a parser that treats a comma as a thousands separator, so 05:34:31,94 became 3,194 seconds — and that value was used as the slew target. The same type of defect set a pixel size of “4,63” in the equipment profile to zero while the dialog reported “saved”, sent “1,23” to the quality analyser’s Python, and built the Gaia query for colour calibration as CIRCLE(’ICRS’, 123,45, 41,27, 2), which Gaia rejects. On Windows with comma decimals, colour calibration therefore always reported “0 catalogue stars”. All of these now accept either separator, and every number sent to another program is written with a point.
body.p_6: When a mount cannot report which side of the pier it will use, the program falls back to a rule: past the meridian and still on the pre-flip side, the flip is due. The rule checked the wrong side. The convention was measured on the ASCOM simulator: two hours east of the meridian it reports pierWest, two hours west it reports pierEast. The old rule returned “not due” while the telescope tracked towards the pier, and “due” again right after a correct flip. It now uses the measured convention. The same test confirmed that the declination-axis sign used by the tracking loop was already correct.
body.h2_5: Stacking: GPU Option Disabled Other Settings
body.p_7: The “GPU acceleration” option is enabled by default. The GPU path implements only the final combination step, so with it enabled the program skipped drizzle, normalisation, quality weighting and automatic rejection without notice, computed “Sum” as a mean, and for median and sigma-clipping used only the first 256 frames — while reporting every frame as accepted. Settings the GPU path cannot handle are now processed on the CPU instead. Local normalisation had a separate fault: in a tile of empty sky it fitted a slope to noise and clamped it to 0.1, scaling each frame’s data down by a factor of two to ten. It now matches each tile by median and spread.
body.p_8: The remote-access tunnel wrote a log line for every connection into a pipe that was never read; once the pipe was full, the tunnel stopped working while still reporting itself as running. The pipe is now read, and the tunnel, like the MCP server, is closed with the program, including after a crash. A damaged settings file could also leave the web credentials empty, and an empty user name and password then matched each other. Empty credentials are now never accepted; they are regenerated and saved, and the settings file is written atomically.
body.p_9: Each fix has a test that fails on the old code and passes on the new, and each test was confirmed to fail on the old code: 22 tests for this first group. A second, independent review of the fixes alone found four mistakes in them — among them the missing site, Canon RAW files that would have been renamed .fits, and two scheduler sessions able to run at once — all corrected before the commit. The full suites pass, including 18 tests on 564 real NGC 2903 frames.
body.p_10: The scheduler uses the imaging camera. Apply and RUN PLAN perform their stated actions. Comma decimals are parsed correctly. The fallback flip rule matches the measured pier sides. The GPU path no longer drops settings. The tunnel no longer stalls, and empty credentials are rejected.
body.p_11: None of this has been tested under a real sky yet. These fixes are in the source and will ship in the next installer; v1.4.11, currently available, does not contain them.
body.p_12: A crash is reported immediately. A button that reports success without acting may go unnoticed until it is used during an observing session. This audit was intended to find such cases beforehand.

article.headline: October Audit, Part 2: Safety Park, Meridian Flip, Polar Alignment and Object Search Fixes
article.deck: The second part of the October audit: a safety park that did not stop the tracking loop, a polar alignment that compared against the J2000 pole, a failed meridian flip that resumed imaging, and an object search in which a request for the Sun returned the Sunflower Galaxy (M63).

sidebar.title: Polar Alignment
sidebar.stat_label: between the J2000 pole and the pole of date
sidebar.stat_desc: The three-point alignment compared the mount’s axis with the J2000 pole. Its quality grades start at 30″. A correctly aligned mount was graded “Poor”, and following the suggested adjustment would have moved it about nine arcminutes off.

body.p_1: The first part of this audit covered buttons that reported success without acting. This part covers the functions that protect the telescope, locate the celestial pole, and find objects by name, several of which produced incorrect results without reporting an error.
body.h2_1: Safety Park With Other Motion Still Active
body.p_2: When an ASCOM safety monitor reports unsafe conditions, the program stops the scheduler and the imaging sequence and parks the mount. It did not stop closed-loop tracking corrections, model-rate tracking, PHD2 guiding or dome slaving. On many drivers, a rate correction or guide pulse during the park slew aborts the park, and a roll-off roof will not close over a mount that is not parked. Dome slaving also kept turning the dome towards the mount while the mount moved to its park position. All four are now stopped before the park. A rotating dome’s shutter still starts closing first, since stopping the loops can take a few seconds; the independent review of this fix found that the first version had delayed the shutter.
body.p_3: A weather station connected over ASCOM Alpaca was only read for its sky-quality value. Its rain and wind readings now trigger the same stop-and-park after two consecutive unsafe readings. Humidity, cloud and dew limits only produce a warning, because these conditions are common at night and not in themselves dangerous to the equipment.
body.h2_2: Failed Meridian Flip No Longer Resumes Imaging
body.p_4: When a meridian flip failed — the pier side did not change, or the slew had not finished after five minutes — the flip manager switched tracking off and then resumed the imaging sequence. A slew still running after five minutes was not stopped. Now the slew is aborted, imaging stays paused, and a message reports the reason. The “pause N minutes before the flip” setting, which was previously not read, now holds the sequence between frames until the target has crossed the meridian. A manual flip used to wait a fixed two seconds for “the current exposure to finish”; it now waits for the exposure to complete.
body.pull_quote_1: After a failed flip the telescope’s position is uncertain, so the program now stops and reports the reason instead of resuming.
body.pull_cite_1: On the callback that resumed imaging after a failure
body.h2_3: Polar Alignment: Fixed 45° Latitude and J2000 Pole
body.p_5: The polar-alignment window read its latitude from an interface field that does not exist, so it always used 45° north, and it was never given a longitude — which, according to a comment in the code, gives the wrong knob directions about half the time. It compared the mount’s axis with the J2000 pole. If the mount refused one of the three rotations, the next image showed the same field, the three positions nearly coincided, and the result could show as 0″ error. It now takes the site from the mount or the Weather tab and refuses to run on a placeholder site, precesses each solved position to the equinox of date, and stops with a message when a rotation is refused or the three positions are too close together to define an axis.
body.p_6: Object names were searched catalogue by catalogue, Messier first, including partial matches. “Sun” is part of “Sunflower Galaxy”, so a remote request for the Sun returned M63, and the solar-safety check, which blocks slews to the Sun, was never triggered. An exact name match in any catalogue now takes precedence over a partial one, and partial matches must be whole words. Apostrophes and hyphens are ignored, so “cats eye” still finds the Cat’s Eye.
body.p_7: The Caldwell, Herschel 400 and Collinder catalogues had their constellation table shifted — Cepheus showed as Circinus, Cassiopeia as Cetus — and every galaxy was labelled “Unknown”. The table was rebuilt from the catalogue files, whose comments name every index. It follows the byte order of the abbreviations, so CMa comes before Cae. These objects also could not be found by voice, because the lookup was case-sensitive; this is fixed.
body.p_8: Periodic error. The PEC export wrote the measured error where the file format expects the correction, so uploading it would have doubled the error. The worm period could also only be detected as 512 s or 341 s for the 12-minute logs the program records. Both are fixed, and a 400, 480 or 600 s worm period is now detected within 3 %.
body.p_9: Horizon. The safety horizon used 0 to mean “no point found”, but 0° is north; every sector next to north fell back to the global 10° limit instead of the profile’s horizon.
body.p_10: Calibration. “Darks before, flats after” took the whole calibration set twice, including flats at night. The calibration wizard took its dark-flats at a fixed 0.5 s regardless of the flat exposure, and never sent the selected binning or offset to the camera.
body.p_11: Mosaic. The end of each panel was treated as the end of imaging, which hid the Stop button for the remaining panels, and a Stop pressed during a slew was ignored for the whole next panel.
body.p_12: Other. Crash recovery was never offered after a real crash. The web password could not be changed, although the messages indicated where to change it. An overnight batch queue stopped after its first job, waiting for a click on a “job completed” dialog.
body.p_13: The pier-side convention was measured on the ASCOM simulator rather than assumed. The catalogue, PEC, horizon, calibration-timing and mosaic fixes have tests that fail on the old code and pass on the new. The safety, flip and dialog fixes are covered by tests that inspect the source code, because exercising them requires a mount and a window. A second independent review of this batch found several more problems in the fixes themselves — including the delayed dome shutter and a polar alignment that would have accepted the placeholder site — and they were corrected before the commit.
body.p_14: Unsafe conditions stop all tracking, guiding and dome-slaving commands before the park. A failed flip stops instead of resuming. Polar alignment uses the actual site and the pole of date. “Sun” resolves to the Sun. The SmartHand catalogues are labelled correctly. PEC, horizon, calibration and mosaic follow their settings.
body.p_15: None of it has been tested under a real sky or on a real dome. The licence check remains symmetric and is pending a decision, since changing it would invalidate existing keys. These fixes are in the source and will ship in the next installer, not in v1.4.11.
body.p_16: Each of these defects was a small, plausible-looking line of code. Together they affected whether the telescope is actually parked and pointed correctly, rather than only reported as such.
